en: {The Spandapradīpikā composed by Utpalācārya}:
That which touches the levels of the supreme and the non-supreme, and from whose volition [arise] dissolution and emergence;
We bow to that which is known as vibration, whose nature is consciousness, the Lord of Power, our own innate strength.
Having bowed to my Guru, whose true nature shines forth as the play of non-conceptual wisdom,
I shall speak a few words endowed with logical reasoning for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, as requested by seekers.
Other forms of knowledge exist that provide immediate results, yet they do not grant ultimate happiness;
the knowledge of the liberated self, however, is like nectar among all delicious flavors, for it conquers death.
The wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) is indeed unique among gems that possess qualities;
just as the sun alone among luminous bodies is the destroyer of all darkness, so it is with this gem.
Born from Trivikrama— the best of the twice-born who dwells in the station of Nārāyaṇa—
for the sake of favoring living beings, Utpala explains the *Spanda*.
Since the wish-fulfilling gem of the Self is concealed by the dense darkness of illusion (māyā) and is therefore not seen, the *Spandapradīpikā* must be grasped in order to attain it.

This is indeed the traditional teaching here: that secret which has come down through the mouths of the perfected ones was obtained by Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭendu from his teacher Vasugupta for the sake of his disciples.
For the sake of easy comprehension, he has here composed a summary in fifty *anuṣṭubh* verses;
and although its meaning has already been made manifest by the moonlight of [his own] commentary, it is nonetheless slightly clarified by this.
Those of dull vision, situated in the midst of the night of delusion, do not perceive the Truth even then;
therefore, I shall today illuminate it for them by myself with the subtle lamp at the end.
When, impelled by the unfolding vibration of my own essential nature through my own act of arising,
I proceeded as if under the influence of another, then this was not begun out of pride.
(This is a collection of verses. Here, first of all,
[the author sets forth] the connection (*sambandha*), the title (*abhidhāna*), the subject matter (*abhidheya-viṣaya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the ultimate purpose (*prayojana-prayojana*).
The "purposes" are said to be six; for without them, listeners would simply disregard the treatise and fail to apply effort toward it. Indeed, it has been stated right here:
"One should examine reality with diligence and respect."

Without the scripture, there would not even be a mere investigation into what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, let alone the examination of reality. Thus it has been said in the *Āgamarahasyastotra*:
If you had not personally manifested your primordial form, you would not have spoken of that most secret reality; otherwise,
the three worlds would certainly have remained blind and mute.
For an entire eon, he would have remained in a state of total inconsistency.
Even in the *Ṣāḍguṇyaviveka*:
"Either you yourself are directly the scripture, for that very intellect is yours;
having transmitted [it] through the medium of words, it refines those who are qualified."
In the *Pañcarātra-śruti* as well, it is said:
"Just as one might ascend a palace by means of a staircase, or cross a river by means of a boat,
even so the Blessed Lord, the Teacher, is to be understood through the scripture alone."

In this regard, the connection between these treatises is fivefold: supreme (*para*), great (*mahat*), divine (*divya*), non-divine (*divyetara*), and mutual (*itaretara*). Among these, the connection here is generally that between a perfected being (*siddha*) and a human being, which is the non-divine type. Now...
It is characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier. The signified is the meaning; the signifier is the treatise (*śāstra*).

Here, the meaning designated as "vibration" (*spanda*) is the signified. Because it signifies that [meaning], the treatise also receives this name through metaphorical usage. This is the meaning of the word *spanda*.
Although this was stated by means of reasoning alone in the first verse, it is nevertheless expressed here along with the meaning of the verbal root.
[The root] *spadi* means "to move slightly.
*Spanda* is derived from *spandana*. As for this [reality], which is without waves, its *spandana*—its vibration—is as follows:
That which is the simultaneous, non-conceptual state of being oriented toward all things belonging to the Supreme Self—
from that [arises]:
"The flashing emergence of intuition (pratibhā), which consists of the tranquilized sixfold qualities."
And that [power] is the Lord of the strength of his own self, whose nature is consciousness and who is designated as "vibration" (spanda).

Therefore, the manifestation of power (*vibhavodaya*) was described in the *Rahasyastotra* by my maternal grandfather, the teacher Mahābala— whose name is true to its meaning— beginning with the words "In wrath," and so forth. It is said:
In the *Iśvarapratyabhijñā*: "And that which is this intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), colored by the succession of various objects,
is the Great Lord, the cognizer whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness."
Because it is all-pervasive, it is the universal; and because it is common to all, it is also the universal. Its vibration is preceded by the universal, and that pure Self is Śaṅkara.
Śiva is known by such designations as Bhāva, Svabhāva, Tattva, and Jñāta.
Furthermore, *cit*, consciousness (*saṃvit*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and awakening (*bodha*) are synonyms. This very [consciousness],
because its nature is that of unobscured *cit*,
has an unrestricted flow unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, and is non-dual.

The Lord of the Wheel of Powers (Śakticakreśvara), for whom one’s own experience is the sole means of valid cognition, is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) by virtue of being the wish-fulfilling gem of the self (*ātmacintāmaṇi*). If it is asked, "Why is he a wish-fulfilling gem? [the answer is]: from the scripture. For it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
The wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) is not perceived as having any inherent nature of its own; nevertheless, it produces whatever is desired. In this same way, Brahman possesses all powers.
And in the *Paramārthasāra*:
"In whatever form the Blessed One is worshipped,
having become that very form, he approaches [the devotee] like a wish-fulfilling gem."
Even though it is of a single nature due to its own essence, cognition assumes manifoldness even in its awakening;
the power of cognition, through its volitions, is like the fortune of a wish-fulfilling gem.

And the author of this treatise has designated it by the names *Śiva* and *Śaṅkara*, which are significant terms (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) intended to convey its quality of producing ultimate welfare; however, in reality...
It is indeed nameless. And this verse concerning non-duality was spoken by Siddhanātha:
"Of a reality that is empty of existence, ungraspable, and devoid of form..."
This which is designated as Śiva is merely a mental construction.
Thus, for the All-pervading Lord, there is no illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) nor any transformation (*pariṇāma*) anywhere;
or, let both exist—nevertheless, there is no contradiction of His nature.
Even within the light of consciousness—
which is of the singular nature of stainless awareness— the assumption of a body occurs through both *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) and *pariṇāma* (transformation).
Even in manifestation, O Acyuta, though you are not of that nature, you appear as such;
in transformation, you are that very same thing, like gold in the form of earrings.

Now, one might ask: how can this [Self] be unobscured, since we perceive it as indeed obscured by the outpourings and fluctuations of the qualities (*guṇas*)—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—and so forth? To this it is replied: for these [qualities], being objects of knowledge, are themselves devoid of independent existence.

However, by taking refuge in the knower, as if having gained a firm footing, those of unawakened intellect— having abandoned their own pure and enlightened nature, and through the notion of "I" having attained identity with the object of desire— [are bound] by their own inherent attributes.

Because they consist of ignorance (*avidyā*), they cause [the soul] to undergo contraction; however, this does not apply to those who abide in their own true nature. And it will be stated further on in this very work:
"The vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth," etc.
And in the examination of the elements:
"For this self, which is variegated by ignorance, its status as an object of cognition remains established;
it does not grasp its own true nature through that variegated self."
And that ignorance, whose nature is unreal, cannot possess the status of a real entity;
for a non-entity cannot bring about the destruction or the modification of a real entity.
Just as no modification or destruction is produced in a piece of rope merely because it is shrouded by darkness,
so too no such change occurs to the Self through ignorance.
Therefore, this Supreme Self has no bondage either from itself or from another;
rather, it is the individual soul (jīva) that is bound by ignorance, and its liberation occurs upon the destruction of that ignorance.
And regarding the application of reality:
by whatever fierce karma sentient beings are bound,
by that very same means they are liberated from the bondage of existence.
In the conjunction of the *kula*,
the falling of living beings is held to be by that very same means their rising;
by what one is bound through ignorance, by that very same thing one is liberated through knowledge.
In the same way, I too [have seen]:
by that very thing through which the dull-witted sink, the wise cross over suffering;
a lump of iron sinks in water, yet that same iron, fashioned into a vessel, floats.
And in the Gītās, such a means is demonstrated here through reasoning:
"Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness,"
In the same way, he into whom all desires enter attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
Likewise,
one whose self is disciplined, moving among sense objects with the senses that are free from passion and hatred and brought under his own control, attains serenity.
Furthermore:
For those who have not abandoned their self-identity, yet do not grasp at sense objects,
and who have realized the ultimate truth— liberation exists even while they are still living.
And these very [states] are the vibration of this Self, like an actor assuming another form.
And it has been said by the Lord of Yogins in the *Cicchaktisaṃstuti*:
"Thus, through Your activity and through Your cessation, the other [worlds] arise."
Since they enjoy those very principles through it, therefore those [principles] are indeed your vibration.
To provide an illustration for this effect despite its dissimilarity, he says:
"Just as smoke rising from fire appears in various forms as it moves through the sky,
so too is this creation of Viṣṇu, born of his own nature, in the form of duality."
Having consumed the mass of nectar, even though he was previously without food, he attained a physical form;
yet when the sun of awakening has risen, the dew-like state returns to its own inherent nature.

Enough with this excessive detail, for fear of making the book too voluminous. Here, this very point is investigated until its conclusion: the purpose of the treatise is precisely the exposition of the means and the goal; and from the realization of that [exposition], there follows the attainment of the nature of the goal.

That alone is the ultimate purpose; this is its independent vision. By the reasoning previously stated, its status as a propounder of non-duality, arising from the totality of all scriptures, is indeed unassailable; for it is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Through ascending the stages of vibration (*spanda*) in the sequence beginning with *paśyantī*, one attains the manifestation of speech.
And it is said in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*:
"From the root of consciousness, from the pillar of knowledge whose leaves are the phonemes, Sarasvatī [emerges]."
Flowing from the east, sounding with a roar, and possessing holy bathing places, it proceeds onward.
That Power, proceeding from you, sustains the universe by its vigor;
returning to you again, it contracts that very manifestation.
Assuming forms and names corresponding to her functions,
she carries out the wondrous course of the entire universe, both moving and unmoving.
And without that [consciousness], existence itself does not exist for any proponent; therefore, they remain already refuted.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"In the Great Lord, who is the agent, the knower, one's own self, and primordially established..."
"Who, being a conscious self, would perform either a negation or an establishment?
This also applies here to those who, out of delusion, hold contrary views; for them, this follows:
just as some regional king [might act] in relation to a universal monarch...
If, immediately after requesting some means such as the fourfold army and so forth, one desires to wage war with that very person out of a wish to conquer his empire,
it would lead only to one's own destruction; the same applies to those [who act] in this way.
Thus, its invincibility is established even in this manner.

Now, the author of the compendium (*saṃgraha-grantha*), having internalized the entire meaning of the foremost treatise (*agrya-grantha*) for the purpose of completing his own work, [proceeds] to praise the chosen deity.
A verse has been introduced; its meaning, though already suggested in the previous verse, is now stated at length:
"We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), by whose opening and closing of his eyes the dissolution and emergence of the world occur. (1)
We praise and bow to that Blessed One, Śaṅkara.

He is called Śaṅkara because he bestows *śam*—meaning welfare, excellence, or happiness—consisting of worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). He is the stainless, intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva*).
It was previously introduced as that which is to be explained; for here, liberation is indeed the state of being liberated while living (jīvanmukti).
And it will be stated further on in this very work, in the passage beginning with "he who possesses such consciousness," and so forth.
And these two are also inherent within her; for she consists of the nature of being a knower, an agent, an enjoyer, and a sovereign. And it has been stated here:
"Then this is her uncreated attribute," and so forth.
Likewise,
[it is said] "when, however, in one place," and so forth;
and also in the *Sarvajñabhairava*:
O beautiful goddess, there is no liberation consisting of going elsewhere or staying somewhere;
that which is the severing of the knot of ignorance is called liberation.
Regarding the dharmas of liberation:
the mind itself, when defiled by the afflictions such as passion and the like, is indeed saṃsāra; that very same mind, when freed from them, is called the end of existence.
In the Buddhist [view],
the mind stained by passion and other defilements is saṃsāra; liberation from that is,
in brief, what has been described as nirvāṇa by the Victors who have abandoned all obscurations.
And in the *Nāradasaṃgraha*:
"All conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is saṃsāra; there is no other bondage than conceptual construction.
And for the author of the treatise, it is for the sake of awakening to one's own true nature (*svasvabhāva*).
The bond, the binder, and the bound—these three are not distinct from one another.
Yet the world is incessantly bound by bonds created by its own conceptual constructions.
And in the *Ātmasaptati*:
"In the actual state of things, there is no bondage; in the absence of that, there is no liberation.
Both of these are merely constructed by conceptualization and are nothing at all."

In the *Pañcarātra* as well, it is stated that there are three kinds of defects (*doṣa*): those born of *svabhāva*, which are *tāmasa*; those born of conceptual construction (*vikalpaja*), which are *rājasa*, and so forth, up until:
"By means of that very body, one becomes self-controlled; when one has become the Blessed One (*bhagavadbhūta*), then one is omniscient."
"He becomes all-seeing, the Lord of all, omnipotent," and so forth.
For this very reason, the word *bhagavat* is employed here: "Of complete sovereignty, knowledge, fame, fortune... [and so on].
And because he possesses detachment and liberation, he is remembered as "Bhagavat" (the Blessed One).
For those who possess self-conceit (*mānin*), there is no one worthy of praise apart from the Blessed One.
In this context, "praise" consists precisely in entering into His essential nature;
indeed, non-difference alone is intended here. Otherwise, who would be the praiser, and who the object of praise? What [distinction could there be]?
Or rather, this praise is contradictory to non-duality (*advaita*), just as it is like overstepping one's own shadow;
and it has been said:
When one knows the object of knowledge by bringing it to the state of one's own nature,
then what would remain as "knowability," or what would remain as the supreme "state of knowing"?
In this case, however, the difference is merely one of words; even that [difference] is rooted in conceptual construction (vikalpa), for it has been said:
"Words have their origin in conceptual construction, and conceptual constructions have their origin in words."
Just as in the expression "the head of Rāhu," or as in "a stream of clarified butter."
Furthermore: That which is non-different in self-awareness, when it is expressed as something else,
appears as if it were different once it has reached the domain of verbal expression.

Without them, even worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) cannot be carried out. It is stated in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*: "Speech alone is the cause of this universal activity; and this is logical, not merely a scriptural tradition."
In this world, there is no action whatsoever that exists without mental construction,
nor is there any conceptualization that exists without speech.
It has already been stated that this too is the root of awakening. Furthermore, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"In the past, having himself become the universal form of unwavering consciousness..."
All those entities produced by sound, whether subtle or extremely subtle;
But for one who perceives the word "general cognition" as having attained oneness,
when [objects] arise from volition and so forth, they appear directly before him.
Of the category of objects consisting of sound and form, sound is remembered as the supreme;
established on the path of volition, it clearly flashes forth while remaining within.
O Sage, know that the sound which arises over an object, as well as those arising from the efforts of the channels of consciousness, wind, and the organs, is the *madhyama* [speech].
That which is manifested through the relationship of the signified and the signifier is called the gross;
it is that which attains manifestation among all things, whether visible or invisible.
But that [consciousness], being even more gross, remains present in all worldly transactions;
furthermore, whether arising from the body, from speech, or from the mind, it has emerged [as such].
O Lord, there is not even that worldly convention in which you are not the foremost.
Thus, this is established. It was said, "We praise Him. Who is He?

He from whose opening (*unmeṣa*)—that is, from His manifestation as the primary cause—the arising, the origin, and the continuous succession of the entire universe proceed; and from whose closing (*nimeṣa*)—that is, from His state of rest—dissolution and absorption likewise occur. Not... [the sentence continues].
Indeed, for this world that is distinct from Him, there is neither arising nor passing away;
rather, arising and passing away are simply the expansion and the cessation of the Lord’s power.
And it has been stated by the Siddhas: [The verse follows: "The expansion of His power is His arising; its cessation is His passing away."

"The entire world arises within the form of Your stainless consciousness at the time of its emergence; it sets once again when [that consciousness] is established in its own true nature. Thus it was also stated by the author of the treatise in the *Tattvavicāra*:
He whose very self consists of arising and passing away, bound by the expansion and contraction of power (śakti), is to be known as Śiva, the instigator of all states of being.
Even in the hymn on the girdle (-),
it is clearly evident that the creation and dissolution of the world consist merely in the opening and closing of the eyes of Your intention;
thus, Your greatness shines forth most manifestly.
By means of the manifestation of various emanations.

That power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which consists of the essence of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) and whose nature is expansion, is described as "volition" (*saṅkalpa*); it is indeed called "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*) in the *Svatantraka*.
Wherever there may be desire, knowledge proceeds there;
from the conjunction of action and instrument, the emergence of the object occurs.

And its cessation is *nimeṣa*. Although it should have been stated as "arising and dissolution" (*udaya-pralaya*), the fact that it was stated as "dissolution and arising" (*pralaya-udaya*) was due to the fear of breaking the meter. Furthermore, the term *unmeṣa* is placed first because, when reversed, the word *unmeṣa* signifies auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
And because it is the beginning of creation,
since there is no objective entity to be denoted, there is consequently no bondage to existence here through the sequence of words.
The position of those who assert [the correspondence] according to numerical order would be inferior.

By these two, His causality regarding the creation and dissolution of the universe, as well as worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), are proclaimed. Therein, from *unmeṣa* (expansion) comes manifold enjoyment;
from *nimeṣa* (contraction) comes liberation, which is the state of being free from waves [of mental fluctuation]. Furthermore, of what nature is He?
Regarding the phrase "the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers":
the one power of the All-pervasive Lord, known as Will (icchā), is first divided into two, called Knowledge (jñāna) and Action (kriyā).
Thus, that manifoldness is expressed by the word "cakra. As it is said in the *Mālinīvijaya*:
"That power of the Creator of the world which is declared to be inherent (*samavāyinī*)."
That goddess assumes the nature of desire in him who wishes to create.
Listen to how even a single entity comes to possess multiplicity:
it should be understood with absolute certainty that "it is thus, and not otherwise."
When she makes known [the will] here in this world, saying, "Let all this be so," and is oriented toward action, she is called the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti).
At that very moment, she is born; her performing various [actions] therein is called "activity" (kriyā).
Thus, although she is of two forms, she again attains multiplicity through further divisions.
"By the power of the limiting adjuncts of objects, the Sovereign Lady (Īśvarī) becomes like a wish-fulfilling gem;
therein she assumes motherhood as the garland of fifty phonemes. Thus, the "wheel of powers" (śakticakra) is the group of mothers (mātṛvarga), and that is the primary [meaning].
It is fourfold. And it has been said:
"The divisions are Khecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī;
the wheel of power (śakticakra), established in the speech of Parā and the others, is fourfold."
Likewise:
"Bliss, Will, Knowledge, and Action—this is the tetrad beginning with Khecarī.
Thus [it is said].
Whatever its manifestation (*vibhava*), power (*vibhūti*), or expansion (*vistara*) may be, it also has an origin (*prabhava*).
It is called "origin" (*prabhava*) because it is that from which [something] originates (*prabhavati*); that is, the place of birth, from which all powers arise.
The state of being Śakti arises from the realization of the pervasive power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*); and that [power] is indeed non-different from it.
For it is stated in the *Śrījaya*:
"Of the pure conscious self whose body is liberated from the [lower] principles (*tattva*)."
"That great bliss which arises is indeed the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti.
And in the Viṣṇuyāmala: "Because of the utterance 'Protect! Protect! and because of protection therein, they possess His very form."
Through contact with the higher and lower powers, and by taking refuge in one's own true nature.
"The foremost Dānavas were slain and supreme valor was manifested;
for that reason, they are called 'Mothers' (mātaraḥ) because they are the cause of the origin of the universe. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, the author of the treatise has stated that their nature consists of a body of consciousness (*vijñāna-deha*).

Or rather, enough of this; what is the use of revealing the true nature of these secrets that have entered the mouths of the Yoginīs? And as for the powers (*śaktis*), whether they be the Khecarīs and so forth, or those beginning with Will (*icchā*) and so forth, or those beginning with the Supreme (*parā*) and so forth, or those beginning with Aghora and so forth, or those beginning with Vāmā and so forth, or those beginning with Brāhmī and so forth—[they are all one].
Or rather, they may be those taught by the Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, Sauras, Buddhists, and others;

or else, as stated in the passage beginning with "arising from the mass of sounds" (śabdarāśi), let them be of the nature of the letters starting with 'a' or of the nature of the instruments (karaṇa) that are about to be described. This much [is the point].

The purpose here is to demonstrate that for all these [deities], the Blessed Lord alone, whose nature is vibration (*spanda*), is the source. And so it is stated in the *Māyāvāmana-saṃhitā*: "Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, Buddha," and so forth.

In its formal aspect (*rūpatayā*), the Blessed One alone— the cause of all— is declared to be worshipped through various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), accompanied by the respective circles of his powers (*śakti-cakra*). And it is said in the *Kulayukti*:
O Maheśvarī, whether in Vedānta, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Saura, Bauddha, or even other systems, there is indeed only one supreme Self; He is the knower, and He is the object of knowledge.
And furthermore:
We praise Him, by whose opening and closing of his eyes the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur.
By this much, everything would have been said regarding the manifestation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) throughout the entire universe;
for it is stated in the secret scriptures (*rahasyaśāstra*):
"Power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*)—these two alone are said to be the categories of reality (*padārtha*)."

"And all the world consists of powers (śakti), while the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the possessor of power (śaktimān). As for the phrase "originating from the manifestation of the wheel of powers" that was introduced, it is for the purpose of enumeration, due to the intentional nature of the great poet. And it has been said:
In the utterances of great poets, there exists another reality altogether that is manifested within the sound;
it shines forth as something exceeding the well-known constituent parts, just as *lāvaṇya* (aesthetic charm) does in women.
Therefore, this alone is the means by which the expansion and emergence of the powers occur within;
by taking hold of that strength, their mastery is attained without delay.
And it has been said here: "But through contact with the power of the Self, a person may become equal to That.
This state which stands before us must be examined with care as the reality.
From this point forward, the wise should apply this principle everywhere here.
Thus [ends the first section]. || 1 ||
Now, one might ask: "How can there be the state of Śaṅkara within the Self during the state of transmigratory existence?
To remove the fault arising from such a doubt, it is said:
"That in which all this effect resides and from which it has emerged..."
Because its nature is unobstructed, there is no cessation of it anywhere.
In that *spandatattva* (the principle of vibration), this entire world characterized as an effect exists in the form of consciousness, having the nature of power (*śakti*),
because the effect pre-exists [in the cause] during the state of dissolution (*nimeṣa*). And because of this...

Having emerged and attained manifestation in the state of unfolding (*unmeṣa*), because its form is unobstructed— due to the reason that its nature is not veiled by way of being of the nature of consciousness—
there is no obstruction anywhere; for [it is] of the nature of the object of cognition itself.
Therefore, the seer itself does not exist; thus, the nature of the knower remains unobscured even in both states.
And it has been said:
"Just as there is variety in gold ornaments without any loss of its own [golden] nature."
Thus, for you whose essential nature is eternal, there exists likewise this universal form.
Just as gold that has lost its form exists in the state of a mass,
so too for you, whose object of knowledge has dissolved, there is the nature of pure consciousness.
Even in the realization of knowledge,
space is the support of the universe, yet the universe does not become the space.
Knowledge is infinite like space, while the object of knowledge is limited like the universe.
Just as space has no obstruction by anything else because of its all-pervasiveness, so too this cognition is unobstructed.
Thus [ends the second].
If cessation were not to occur upon the withdrawal of all mental functions,
how could there be non-cessation during states such as waking and the rest?
Even as it extends through the various states such as waking and the rest, which are non-different from it, it never departs from its own inherent nature as the perceiver. || 3 ||

Even as the distinctions of waking and so forth unfold, and even while they are spreading out, that principle of vibration (*spanda-tattva*) does not at all turn back from its own innate nature, which is the form of the perceiver and whose essence is self-awareness. Why? Because of the reason that it is the perceiver.
For the nature of being a perceiver is common to all three states;
and it has been said:
"This distinction exists only among the states, never in the one who abides in those states."
"Just as [the power] of poison exists in its sprout and so forth, yet there is no difference [between the two].
Thus, the awareness of both waking and dreaming is well-established for everyone;
even in deep sleep, there is the experience—even for an ignorant person—of the subsequent time, such as "I slept happily," and so forth.

Because there is cognition, the cognizer is indeed non-existent. And it has been said: "Just as the moon, though its reflections tremble in accordance with the movement of the water, does not undergo the penetration of action, so it is here with the Supreme Self."

The apprehension of objects by a seer through the senses is called waking;
that which consists of the recollection of objects by the mind without those [senses] is designated as dreaming.
That state in which there is no recollection of objects is declared to be deep sleep;
that which remains as the singular form of pure consciousness is itself the fourth state (turyatā).
This verse is intended to refute those who claim that states themselves cannot abide within the universe;
[it does so] by means of arguments such as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
[The verse says: "I am happy, I am miserable, I am impassioned," and so forth—such are the cognitions.
It is clear that these [mental states] exist elsewhere as well, being permeated by conditions such as pleasure and so forth.
Those cognitions, perceptions, or states such as "I am happy" and so forth—

having made it clear that these exist as modifications (*uparāgatayā*) within the cognizer, the substratum of the states, the perceiver of pleasure and the rest, and not apart from those cognitions themselves— [they are established].
They exist, they remain; for without a knower, there is no such thing as cognition. Or rather, having entered into that [knower], they attain identity with it, like rivers entering the ocean.
For it is indeed of momentary cognitions [that this applies], but not of those [cognitions] alone by themselves.
For it has been said:
"Indeed, the relationship of cause and effect, as well as the state of being the sublated and the sublater,
cannot be established without a single cognizer who [perceives] the preceding and the succeeding."
For in that case, validity is established by perception through its momentariness,
because validity is proven by the firmness of the subsequent cognition that follows immediately after.
Furthermore, since there is no apprehension of a universal because of its difference at every moment,
all moments are distinct; what, then, would be the basis for their validity?
Furthermore, since the relation [between the object and its cognition] is not apprehended, what is the status of that means of knowledge?
Or tell me, what is the basis for the falsity of false cognition?
For at another moment, who can prevent silver from appearing in a mother-of-pearl shell?
If that which possesses divided knowledge were the agent, everything would attain the status of being authoritative.
If the establishment of one thing’s own nature were to entail the establishment of another,
then upon the establishment of the nature of a jar, there would be the cognition of a cloth.

The cognition "this is that very same [thing]," which arises over a period of time, cannot be established by momentary entities, because its validity would be sublated [if they were momentary]. Therefore, [the object] is not momentary.
"Recognition, which consists of the recollection of prior consciousness, is eternally established;
therefore, agency is attributed only to the self (ātman), whose nature is eternal.
What more need be said?
Because there is no single cognizer, because of momentariness, and because of the lack of certainty,
even a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would be non-valid for the Buddhists, as it would be without a basis.
Thus it is said; and it is stated in the *Bauddhāyana-saṃhitā*:
"In cognition, there is no relation of cause and effect, for it perishes in a single moment."
If a second moment does not exist, how could there be a seed of memory?
How can that which is its producer be both destroyed and not destroyed, or both increased and not destroyed?
If that which is destroyed possesses the capacity to produce, then there would be a continuity of existence arising from non-existence.
If, however, it remains as a producer without having perished, its momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is abandoned;
for if it were to persist into a second moment, it would remain even for a hundred [moments].
If it were a producer, that which has half-perished would not reach non-existence in the other half;
therefore, all entities are stable and do not deviate from their own nature.
Those [cognitions] which are well-established regarding the object of self-awareness are not momentary;
furthermore, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator cannot exist without a definitive determiner.
"For indeed, the sublation of the error consisting in the cognition of silver occurs in the case of mother-of-pearl, and not otherwise.

Therefore, cognition is eternal and one; it is not many and momentary. And in the *Satkāryasiddhi*: [The relevant verse follows: "If the effect were non-existent [prior to its production], then even the blind man would perceive form, etc., because there would be no distinction [between the capacities of the sighted and the blind]. Furthermore, since the cause does not exist, what could produce what? Moreover, if the effect were non-existent, it would follow that everything could arise from everything."
For there is no mutual cognition by means of consciousnesses that are restricted to themselves;
therefore, [consciousness] is not skilled in grasping prior and subsequent states.
A single cognizer engages in worldly transaction through manifold mental states;
and likewise in recognition, [there is the experience] of those who are mutually distinct yet cognizant of one another.
The worldly condition of living beings would perish, born as it is from the continuous succession of cognitions.

If Maheśvara were not the one who has internalized within himself the infinite forms of the universe, he could not be the singular embodiment of consciousness endowed with the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance].
Even in the Gītā, it is said: "From Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
Enough, then, with chewing on the stones of fallacious reasoning! Furthermore, in what kind of state [is he]?
In the cognizer who is interwoven as the nature of the knower throughout states such as pleasure and so forth— just as a thread is always interwoven through jewels—
he is indeed [present] in all states; for he who is "I" is that very one.

He who was happy before is the very same person who is unhappy today; this is because of the synthesis of memory and recognition, as indicated by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), such as: "I am attached," "I am detached," "I am deluded," "I am awakened," or "I possess wealth and so forth."

But surely, in this way, he would possess veils (*sāvaraṇa*). This is not true; for those [veils], being of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), are impermanent. Furthermore, because they are distinct from the cognizer, they are merely adventitious (*uparāga*) to him through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). And it has been said by Bhartṛhari:
Just as no modification or destruction is produced in a piece of rope merely because it is covered by darkness,
even so no such change occurs to the Self through ignorance.
And in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*:
"Just as the innate form of a crystal, due to its extremely pure nature,
is always perceived only when it is colored by another."
Likewise, O Blessed One, your body, though attached to existence,
is not perceived as separate from those [elements] due to its utter purity.
"It is not by this much that this crystal does not exist separately from the colorant; nor is your stainless body devoid of the nature of existence.
Thus [it is said]: And likewise:
O Lord, even during an eclipse, this [consciousness] does not abandon its purity;
for how could that which is called consciousness resort to anything else after having abandoned its own nature?
Moreover, if it were to follow after another form even without reaching that [other] form,
then it would indeed be seen as having that form, since the cause for such a thing is possible.
Likewise, in this very context:
this experience is always pure, variegated by every form;
even at the time of shifting to another form, it remains stainless.
Just as a cloth that is white by nature becomes dyed red by some color, and having attained that state of whiteness, it might again take on another color; so too is this case.
Thus, consciousness, which is pure by nature, when colored by a particular form,
remains purely so in the interval between the abandonment of that form and the transition to another.
Likewise,
the undivided nature of consciousness— whether in relation to blue, yellow, pleasure, or pain—
is differentiated by conceptual construction through the acquisition of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
And he states the nature of that which is distinct from those:
"Where there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the grasped nor the grasper, and even no state of delusion—that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality. (5)

That reality of vibration (spandatattva) exists in the ultimate sense because of its eternity; wherein there is no suffering— whether internal and so forth— and no pleasure derived from sense objects,
no object of perception such as a jar or a cloth, and no perceiving subject such as "I" or "this."

The statement "I grasp" refers to the nature of the ordinary, conceptualized ego (ahaṅkāra), because that ego is essentially composed of ignorance (*avidyā*). However, by this, it is not meant that there is an absence of the subject who grasps, whose nature is that of the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*).
Because that [reality] is the goal to be attained (*upeya*). And it has been said in the *Tattvagarbha*:
"In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped (*grāhya*) nor any grasper (*grāhaka*);
for, apart from that [reality], it is perceived as having its own manifestation, though appearing as if without its own manifestation."
If that is so, then that state is either a stone-like dullness or simply emptiness.
To this it is replied: "Nor even does the state of dullness exist," because it lacks any form whatsoever. And it has been said by the Sage:
Just as at the time between cold and heat there is neither heat nor cold,
even so there exists for the All-pervading Lord a state that is devoid of both pleasure and pain.
And in the hymn it is said: "Just as the sun rises in the sky without [previously existing] objects,
so too does the Blessed One, the Sun of Existence, arise by his own power without any object of cognition."
Likewise,
the innate state of a universal (sāmānya), from which its particularity has been abstracted,
cannot be pointed out separately; yet, for all that, it does not cease to exist therein.
Just as when an earring or the like is removed, its own inherent state cannot be pointed out as separate [from the gold], yet that does not mean it does not exist therein.
Thus, your state, consisting of pure consciousness, is eternal, innate, pure, undifferentiated by pleasure or pain,
and perceivable through self-awareness.
Nāgārjuna also said:
"It is empty of all objective supports, all phenomena, all principles without exception, and all latent tendencies of the afflictions; yet it is not empty from the perspective of ultimate reality."
Thus it is said;
and in the *Ālokamālā*:
"That which, because of its opposition, allows no room for the activity of darkness..."
That indescribable state, which cannot be known by the senses, is called emptiness (śūnyatā).
Nor, however, does it follow merely from worldly convention that it conforms to the meaning of nihilism.
Thus [ends the verse]. || 5 ||
Regarding this, he states the proof for its non-deludedness and existence by means of a summary verse (*sandānitaka*):
"Since this group of instruments, though itself deluded, acts as if undeluded along with the internal wheel, performing the functions of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal. (6)
One should therefore examine that reality with effort and respect;
for its independence is everywhere innate.
Because, from the principle of Spanda (Spandatattva), this external group of organs— known as the organs of cognition and action— together with the wheel of internal organs,
being specifically characterized by a deluded consciousness, attains its own activity, maintenance, and withdrawal as if it were insentient.
This illustrative example for the cause of such an occurrence is a deceptive gem;
just as, through contact with wind and fire, a mass of iron may appear to be fire itself.
"Just as [fire] is capable of burning, cooking, illuminating, and so forth, so too is this group [of qualities].

Thus, how can that which is capable of imparting consciousness to others be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? This has been stated in the *Ṣāḍguṇyaviveka*: [The relevant verse from the Ṣāḍguṇyaviveka follows here.]
This entire activity of cognition is witnessed by one's own body;
for the body, when not presided over by cognition, merely wallows, being devoid of support.
"For this very reason, even the support of insentient things is understood to be produced by a presiding agent; otherwise, how could a stone remain suspended in the sky?
Therefore, that reality should be investigated with effort and reverence. Effort...

Exertion (*udyoga*) is enthusiasm; respect (*ādara*) is faith (*śraddhā*). In this context, "examination" (*parīkṣaṇa*) refers to acceptance through the penetration of the power of exertion. And it has been said here:
"Therefore, one should always be diligent," and so forth.
And it has been stated by the Siddhas:
"Brahman is invisible like the eye, yet it possesses the capacity for seeing like the eye;
its perception occurs within itself alone, but not as [an external object] such as a jar."

Since this innate, natural, and independent power belongs to him everywhere, he has stated this: "Just as his independence in bestowing consciousness upon instruments and the like is established, so too is it possible [to exercise it] even in the bodies of others through practice. (7)
By His will alone resides the capacity of the instruments; His independence is declared everywhere. Therefore, this very [process] is the method for His enjoyment.
For this [mantra] does not function as an impeller by means of its own desire;
rather, through contact with the power of the Self, the person becomes equal to it.
This person, the individual soul (jīvātman), exists solely as the impeller of the "impulsion of desire"—that is, the impeller of the mechanism of the organs that prompts through desire;
the word *hi* here has the sense of *eva* (only) or the sense of *kevalam* (solely). Furthermore, the particle *api tu* [is used].

Upon the cessation of negation, it reveals its own essential nature. "Self-power" (*ātmabala*) is the power of the Self, which is the nature of unobscured consciousness characterized by omniscience and agency. Through contact with—that is, the mastery of—that [power], one becomes equal to it: omniscient.
The meaning is that he would be the creator of all things. || 8 ||
By this, his complete sovereignty has been described;
yet he speaks of another [state] at another time through the destruction of the agitation consisting of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*). [He says:
"For one who is incapable due to innate impurity, yet desires to act toward what ought to be done..."
When agitation is completely dissolved, then the supreme state is attained.
One’s own innate, beginningless impurity is rooted in ignorance and non-discrimination;

it takes the form of the stain of longing for enjoyment for one who is powerless and whose capacity is contracted. For this very reason, it does not belong to one who is desirous—that is, full of longing—regarding the duties and tasks that ought to be performed.

It occurs even for one who desires an effect. And so it is stated in the Śrīsātvata-tantra: "The pervasiveness of ignorance and the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth [arise] from the Supreme Self's reality (ātmatattva) owing to its dependence upon the wheel of karma."

In the Gītās, this is called by various names such as *prakṛti*, impurity (*aśuddhi*), prior karmic impressions (*prākkarmavāsanā*), *māyā*, *avidyā*, delusion (*bhrama*), infatuation (*moha*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), and stain (*mala*).
And it is said in the Gītā:
"Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
know also that the transformations and the qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti."
Although its beginninglessness is the same [as that of other categories], this is its specific distinction when examined:
namely, that it undergoes dissolution because its nature is *māyā*. As it is said in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*:
"Its very nature as *māyā* consists in this: that its destruction occurs through the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*)."
"For one who has recognized the rope as the reality, one does not again imagine it to be a snake or the like.
And elsewhere: "Whatever second entity exists here other than you..."

"If even that [Self] were brought within the range of discursive inquiry, it would vanish like a city of Gandharvas; therefore, you alone remain as a certainty, and thus you bear the name 'The Residue' (śeṣa). Thus [it is said].
And when the abode of the sense-objects has been consumed through the method of the meditative absorption whose nature is the consumption of the Lord of Knowledge,
you, having reached the state of the All-Eater, remain as the Supreme Eaten One.
And that [impurity] resides within the obstructing self like a magician’s illusion,
just as a column of smoke resides in fire or a film of dirt on a mirror.
Like bubbles upon the water, there is a state of changelessness when those [disturbances] have subsided; however,
when the agitation— a modification born of impurity in the form of the bodily notion of "I"— is dissolved through discernment by contact with the power of the Self.
Then it undergoes dissolution; the meaning is that the supreme state is attained, which is abiding in one's own true nature.
This has been stated in the *Ṣaḍadhātusamīkṣā*: [(-)]

Since actions rooted in delusion are the cause of cyclic existence, by their destruction one is liberated from karma; consequently, one becomes established in one's true nature and supremely tranquil.
In the *Nāradasaṃgraha* it is also said:
"Just as a seed that has been thoroughly roasted does not sprout again in this world,
so for one whose mind is exhausted of conceptual construction, there is no further transmigration."
And that destruction of agitation occurs gradually through practice; for it is said in the *Ātmasambodha*:
"Just as a spark of fire drawn out from its source [blazes up]."
One should proceed slowly toward a true shrine, not hastily;
likewise, even when the mire of ignorance has been cast off,
the embodied soul attains liberation in due time.

In the *Ṣāḍguṇyaviveka*, this much distinction between the individual self (*ātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) is stated: "Though [the individual self] appears divided by that sense of 'I' (*ahaṃyuti*) which is assumed through the contraction produced by ignorance (*avidyā*),
it is in reality non-different from Him, like one who fears a dream."

For one who, though actually fearless, experiences agitation while fearing in a dream— what ultimate difference is there between that [dream] and this [awakened state], which is not distinct from the dream?
For if one realizes that "this fear of mine is indeed false," and reflects upon the true nature of dreams, one is no longer afflicted by that shattered fear.
"Thus, through the contemplation that 'I am indeed composed of you,' one whose knot of egoity has dissolved within you perceives your very self-nature. Thus it is said in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*.
O Mādhava, although this action was performed by you, it is composed of you;
therefore, when the ego-sense has vanished, you alone remain.
The difference of this [self] consists solely in the sense of "I" regarding the self;
if that is dissolved through devotion to You, the difference perishes and unity remains.
He states the qualities of one who abides in his own true nature:
"Then his innate quality, characterized by knowledge and agency, exists;
for he knows and accomplishes everything that he desires. (10)
Then, at that time when all agitation has dissolved, for this Self, its innate and natural quality (*dharma*)— that is, its very nature (*svabhāva*)— becomes established in its own true form;
such is the completion of the sentence.

What kind [of thing]? One who knows is a "knower" (*jña*); the state of being that is "knowing-ness" (*jñatva*). One who acts is an "agent" (*kartṛ*); the state of being that is "agency" (*kartṛtva*). That which is characterized by these two, or that dharma for which these two constitute its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or mark (*cihna*), is it.

It is characterized by the nature of knowing and agency. For, from whatever dharma—or from whatever cause—that which one desires or intends to know, one knows; and that which one wishes to do, one performs, whether for oneself or for another. And this very same dharma is taught in the *Pañcarātra*.
It is expressed by the term "knowledge born of discrimination" (vivekaja-jñāna).
And what is the precursor to its manifestation, by which one becomes all-knowing, a seer of truth, the Lord of all, and possessed of all powers?
And that [consciousness] would exist for him even without the sense-faculties; for it is said in that very same place:
"Just as fire, when burning something, does not take up anything else [as fuel], yet burns by itself with the thought 'I shall burn'; in the same way, this self exists without taking up [anything]."
The Knower, acting without grasping, performs all actions by his own self;
why? Because his nature is consciousness (*bodha*). As it is stated in the *Ṣāḍguṇyaviveka*:
"Consciousness does not depend on anything else for the creation of diverse objects."
The Unborn One creates thousands of forms by mere volition alone.
However, for those who claim that his status as knower, agent, and so forth arises from another source, he would simply not be the Lord (anīśa).
For it is said in the *Āgamarahasya*:
"Even those who designate the Lord as merely the efficient cause..."
"To her who was thus addressed, they offered a handful of sesame seeds and water;
alas, these people proclaim that he has attained the state of a lord of love by approaching another woman."
Therefore, what was stated is correct. || 10 ||
The means for the stabilization of this uncontrived reality is stated:
For one who, beholding that intrinsic nature as its presiding lord, remains as if smiling, from where could such a deceptive path arise? (11)
Beholding— that is, seeing and recognizing— that pure self-nature as the presiding subject, as consciousness itself, and as all-pervasive,
he remains as if smiling, as if overcome with wonder, and as if blossoming; he who thus abides.
With the dissolution of that ignorance, whence could this "evil course"—this contemptible cycle of transmigration—arise from anywhere? This is the completion of the sentence.

And it has been stated in the *Śivasūtras*: [The sūtra follows: "When the Lord is pleased, [the yogin attains] the state of Śiva. (ŚS 2.1) *Note: The specific sūtra cited here corresponds to Śivasūtra 2.1, which reads: "prabhu-prasādāt śivatvam" (Through the grace of the Lord, [one attains] the state of Śiva).*
Wondrousness is the stage of yoga. And its "contemplation" is the experience [of it] by way of being the seer. For it is said in the *Iṣṭopadeśa*:
O son, abandon this house which is seen by the eye;
behold that by which you see, having seen which you perceive everything.
And the author said:
"O you who speak thus among these [people], what indeed do you observe?
One who acts in this way is deluded by the mere trappings of sense-objects; he is one who has not examined what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected."
There is the thought.

Likewise, how could there be for him any pursuit of other wrong paths, such as the art of conceptualization driven by desire? Rather, he would always remain established in his own true nature; and by being established therein, like Īśvara, he possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpa*).

Therefore, it would not exist in this very case; for without practice, even that which is known cannot be accepted as one's own, and without that, how could there be accomplishment? As the Sage has said:
If liberation were to occur through scriptural knowledge alone, without meditative cultivation,
then all living beings would be liberated from physical and mental sufferings.
And likewise, it is stated in the *Yukti*: "For even that which is indicated by the absence of taste in an elixir (*rasāyana*) does not grant success.
Furthermore, it has been said:
O Blessed One, although You are known thus by everyone from cowherds and children to women, You do not grant liberation due to the lack of the proper means;
for the water that quenches thirst does not remain within the cows themselves.
That very same milk would become [something else] again through consumption.
To refute those proponents of emptiness who say this—
"One should contemplate non-existence until one attains identity with it"—
[the author replies]: "Non-existence cannot be contemplated, nor is there freedom from delusion therein."
From the contact with that application, there arose the certainty that "it was so. || 12 ||
Therefore, that [state] should always be known as artificial, like the state of deep sleep;
however, such a state of being remembered does not attain the nature of that true reality.

Non-existence, which is like the horn of a hare, cannot become an object of experience—that is, it cannot attain the status of being experienced—because it is a non-entity. Furthermore, there is no state of non-delusion regarding that non-existence; rather, that state is itself one of delusion.

From the contact with application and the conjunction with desire, there arose the cultivation of its absence— the certainty that "it was past. Because it is remembered by me as a void state that has passed, it is so stated.
That entity by which non-existence is made known neither exists nor does it not exist;
tell me, by what can the true existence of that entity be negated?
"Therefore, that conscious state exists by which everything is manifested.

For this reason, the cultivation of the non-existence of that [consciousness] should always be known as artificial and impermanent. What is it like? It is like the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*); however, it is not truly so.
Just as in the state of delusion, that reality of the Self (ātmatattva) attains the state of being remembered—

that is, it becomes an object of memory— due to its nature as the knower and because it is eternally manifest. Therefore, through the instruction of the Guru, one should [realize] that very reality with devotion.
"It is to be examined," [it is said]. (12–13)
Thus,
there are two states here, distinguished by the subject who remembers and the object to be remembered;
it is for the sake of investigating their permanence or impermanence that this is stated.
And here, there are two states designated as "the state of being an object" and "the state of being an agent.
Among these, the state of being an object is subject to decay, whereas the state of being an agent is imperishable.
In this aforementioned reality of Spanda, there exists a pair of states, a duality of conditions, which is designated as "the state of being the object and the agent" (kārya-kartṛtva),
or known by the names "effect and cause" (kārya-kāraṇa), consisting of the enjoyed and the enjoyer.

The distinction between the seen and the seer, divided by the threefold [states], consists of the nature of the object of knowledge and the knower. Between those two, that which is the state of being an effect is perishable, characterized by arising and destruction;
whereas that which is agency is imperishable and unimpeded, because its essence is consciousness.
For this very reason, only that effort which is directed toward an effect is suppressed here;
when that is suppressed, the ignorant person thinks, "I am destroyed. (15)

In this case, when the external object— the thing to be accomplished— is perishable, that effort directed toward the task, which consists of the activity of the external organs and is oriented toward the accomplishment of the task, is merely lost; it is no longer perceived.

Having become subservient, it remains within its own self, or because the senses are obstructed, they lack the capacity for activity. When that effort has ceased, the ignorant, unawakened person perceives—that is, believes—that "I am dissolved, I am destroyed. But [in reality], it is not so.
There is no destruction of that which has consciousness as its nature. And it has been said:
"There is no destruction of consciousness even when the body has perished;
just as when the sun-crystal is absent, there is no loss to the sun."
Thus [ends the section]. 15.
And why? He says:
"But that internal state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience—its loss could never occur, because nothing else is perceived. (16)

There is indeed the cessation— that is, the disappearance— of the effect itself when it is separated by space, time, and so forth; however, there is no cessation of that inward-turned state which, because it does not project outward, abides in its own nature as its own essence,
characterized by omniscience and other such qualities.

The locus and substratum of qualities—their cessation might at some time occur; it would be possible. Why would it not occur? Because, apart from that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), no second thing is perceived or apprehended. For that alone exists everywhere.
There is perception at all times. This is what was said:
"Among objects delimited by place, time, action, and form, you shine forth as undelimited in nature because of your existence outside of them."
And here [it is said]: "There is no distinction here between omniscience and the like, and knowledge and the like,
because they exist as the very nature of consciousness, which is of the form of pure awareness."

And it is said in the *Ṣāḍguṇyaviveka*: "Among the qualities, knowledge is primary at the beginning and the end; for when reality has been determined by it, the status of sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and vigor is established as being of the nature of dharma."
In the hymn on the girdle:
"Your knowledge is tranquil, its function being awakening; the sovereignty of others has its expansion rising up."
That power which is capable of manifestation and possesses external stability is *bala* (strength).
But when the outward expansion has arisen, it is your own single power, O Hero, which illuminates external objects through its energy; thus, in this way, it is one and the same.
But through external reflection, however, ignorance arises.
In that regard, omniscience is knowledge, for everything indeed arises from it;
because power has satisfaction as its root, while patience lacks that [satisfaction],
awakening is the radiance here, for that is always the root of awakening.
As it has been said:
"That light characterized by radiance which overpowers others is itself to be known precisely because of its nature as consciousness;
for consciousness overpowers the entire world."
"And here, sovereignty is autonomy; for the Lord possesses autonomy.
Thus it has been said:
"He is autonomous in all actions, neither subject to injunction nor beset by obstacles."
Whether you are active or inactive, for that reason you are the Lord.

Vigor is the state of having power that is never lost and the absence of destruction for one who possesses it. As it has been said: "Fortitude consists in remaining firm due to the characteristic of not falling away from the essence of the self."
And this connection of yours with the task arises from vigor, just as [the color] of gold [is inherent];
that power is of infinite capacity, being omnipotent at all times through its inherent efficacy.
Regarding the question of where and for whom its perception occurs, he says: "Its perception is constant and never deviates from the three states;
it belongs eternally to one who is perfectly awakened, but for another, it occurs at the beginning and end [of those states]. (17)

For that yogin whose nature is consciousness, there should be constant perception—that is, experience. Of what kind of yogin? Of one who is always, at all times, perfectly awakened. Of what kind of perception? One that does not deviate from the three states—that is, it persists even throughout the three states of waking and so forth.
That which does not deviate and does not cease throughout the stages of the states is described as such; however, in the fourth state, it is indeed free from error.
And it has been said:
There is no state whatsoever in which consciousness does not abide;
therefore, yogis worship you as the very mass of consciousness.

Furthermore, for another who is slightly awakened and for one who is fully awakened, there is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of those three words beginning with "that" (*tat*). This is what is meant: [it is] "consisting of that" at the beginning—that is, in the prior state—and also at the end.
"The state of the condition [of consciousness] is at the beginning and the end of waking and the fourth [state], according to the tradition.
Alternatively, it means "at the beginning of that, at the end of that, and in the middle of those two," namely waking and dreaming; for these two alone belong to the awakened one.
Manifest apprehension is experience. || 17 ||
And in order to clarify where and how that [manifestation] occurs for him, he says:

"Endowed with the supreme power whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, the All-pervasive Lord shines in two states; elsewhere, however, He consists of pure consciousness alone. (18)

The all-pervading, omnipresent Supreme Self, consisting of consciousness and having the nature of pure awareness, is endowed with supreme power—that is, with most excellent capacity. He shines and manifests within the two states consisting of waking and dreaming. By what kind of power?

By means of its two forms—namely, the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)—its supremacy arises from this very duality of form. For this reason, in these two states, there is a twofold apprehension.
Furthermore, "elsewhere" refers to the pair of states other than those two aforementioned states.

In that which is called deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the fourth state (*turya*), it consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*) and is indeed pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). The meaning is that, due to the absence of any object of knowledge (*jñeya-abhāva*), it is the very nature of knowledge itself. || 18 ||

Regarding the apprehension of that [Self] which was described as existing through the movement of the *guṇas* and so forth, the doubt may arise: "From where does it come? To those who hold this doubt, the following is said:
"Those [entities] whose movement arises from the *guṇas* and so forth, as well as those that are motionless, exist by depending upon the universal movement."
Having attained their own existence, they would constantly be non-obstructive to the wise man. || 19 ||
The qualities (*guṇas*) are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the sense organs (*indriyas*), and the gross elements (*bhūtas*) are also included.
This vibration (*spanda*) consists of the qualities and so forth; it is the vibration of the qualities etc. Those which are its outflows (*niṣyandas*)—
The currents— namely, the specific cognitions characterized by waves of pleasure, pain, and delusion—
have acquired their own existence by virtue of being supported by and resting within the general vibration previously described, which possesses infinite particularities.
They have attained their functional existence. For this very reason, for the wise yogin who has known what is to be known,
these [qualities] would be constantly and eternally non-obstructive, due to the absence of separation from his true nature and the absence of contact with anything else.
The meaning is that they do not obscure their own nature. And it has been stated by the Siddha:

"Just as the measure [i.e., the instrument] of a light-source is not perceived with respect to its object of illumination due to contact, so too consciousness is never manifested in relation to the object of cognition."
And it has already been stated that these are indeed its own vibrations. Also, in the *Mataṅgapārameśvara*:
"This path, which extends from Śiva down to the earth and is exceedingly vast, is to be known as entirely within consciousness, because it is perceived by it."
And in the Gītās:
"For this divine illusion of mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross beyond this illusion."
But for the ignorant one— whose intellect is unawakened— these [defilements], striving to conceal his own true state, cast him onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross. (20)

For that person whose intellect (*dhī*) or understanding (*buddhi*) is unawakened and utterly deluded, these [guṇas]— the vibrations and outpourings from the source— are intent upon obstructing and veiling the state of one’s own abiding nature, which is the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). For he...
At that time, one perceives the self as being of that very nature [impure], and not as having the form of pure awakening. And it has been said:
"Just as a child sees his own clear mirror soiled by his own breath,"
"In the same way, consciousness, having an inert substratum, acts through its own conceptual constructions.
For this very reason, they cause one to fall upon the path of saṃsāra;
they impel one onto the track of the flow of birth and death. Of what sort [is that path]? It is difficult to cross.
"Crossing over with difficulty" means deliverance from that which is therefore terrible and productive of afflictions (*kleśa*).
As it is said in the *Jñānasambodhi*:
"Even though for two who are blind, movement occurs directly by their own power alone..."
Nevertheless, one goes by himself, while the second is led by another.
Those with expansive awakening possess independence even amidst difficulties, like those with eyes; whereas those of dull intellect possess dependence even on level ground, like the blind.
Thus [ends the twentieth].
Now, he states the means for crossing over even for one who is ignorant:
"Therefore, constantly striving for the discernment of the reality of Spanda, even while awake, one attains one's own true nature before long. (21)
Since they are prone to falling [from their state], for this reason, he who is constantly and at all times diligent— having exerted effort through his blossoming nature—
for what purpose? For the sake of discernment, that is, for the clear investigation of the reality of *spanda*.
It is for the purpose of manifesting one's own nature (*svarūpa*). That which is the form of the impeller (*udyoktṛ*) is [the Self]. And it has been stated in the *Śivasūtras*:
"The impulsion (*udyoga*) is Śiva."

Therefore, even while awake—that is, even during the state of waking and amidst external activity—one attains and reaches one's own innate nature (*nijam ātmīyam svabhāvam*) without delay, that is, quickly. This is his discernment: "I am of the singular form of pure consciousness."
And this entire world is indeed my own expansion. As it has been said:
"For one who fully realizes, 'All this is my own manifestation,' there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of mental constructs regarding the Self of the universe."
Even in the *Pañcarātra*, it is said:
"When one perceives all beings within oneself and oneself within them, and [perceives them] as distinct from them, then one is liberated from death and birth."
And elsewhere:
"O you who are stainless and whose sole nature is infinite consciousness, you are perceived by those of pure intellect and attentive mind, whether as the object of knowledge or as the knower."
And in the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*:

"Thus, yoga— having attained the emergence of its own true nature through the destruction of various and manifold delusions— is eternally established in its own self and liberated, due to being devoid of identification with that which is not the self."
One who knows the distinction between the seen and the seer, who pervades the state of worldly existence yet is free from the affliction of disease,
partakes in samādhi even during the period of emergence; such a person is the cause of the glory of true liberation.
Thus [ends the twenty-first].
The description of one's true nature while awake is not perceived by the ignorant;
therefore, the stages of the arising of vibration (*spanda*) are taught, wherein it is perceived.
Whether one is extremely angry or greatly delighted, or while reflecting "What shall I do?",
or while running— whatever step one takes, therein vibration (spanda) is established.
When one, having become exceedingly enraged by the anger ignited by an enemy, goes to whatever state [of mind],

whatever expansive [feeling] he relies upon, or whatever state of longing he touches; or else, when one is thrilled by the sight of a long-absent beloved and so forth, and thus becomes overjoyed, whatever state [of mind]—

One should go toward the form of supreme bliss (*parānanda*) and seize it. Likewise, being agitated by the waves of manifold activities and reflecting and deliberating—thinking "What shall I do?", "I am doing this," or "Shall I do that?"—one enters a state of anxiety; [this is] that state.
He would go and reach a state of certainty; likewise,
by having his mind captivated by his beloved, whether through agitation or by running and running again,
whatever step he takes— that state he ascends— there, at that very step.
The previously mentioned *spanda*, which is the very nature of the Self, is "established," meaning it exists as something clearly perceived. This is what is meant:
wherever, whenever, and by whatever means the dissolution of all powers may occur, [it is there that this nature is established].
"The arising of that [power] occurs here and there as the clearly manifest reality of Spanda. For it is said:
"From anger come all grounds of suffering; from joy come all grounds of happiness."
"The functions of the senses, arising from delusion, rush about thinking, 'What shall I do?
And it is said in the *Vijñānabhairava*:

"In anger, at its end, in fear, in grief, in a thicket, in warding off, in battle, in curiosity, at the end of hunger and so forth— the reality of Brahman is near. Thus it is said in the *Rahasyastotra*.
Those who, though overcome by anger or joy, have resorted to the highest state and reflect upon their action,
and whose touch— though its locus of action is unregulated— is said to bestow power upon the self; they call that movement *spanda*.
"This [state], which possesses omniscience and other qualities, is said to occur elsewhere at the falling away of the *tuṭi*.
Thus, at the falling away of the *tuṭi*, there arise omniscience, omnipotence, universal sovereignty, and so forth.
And this must be examined with care through the instruction of a Guru. (22)
To bring about this very [state], he states another means by way of a specific verse:
"Adopting whatever state [of mind] he might describe to me, I shall certainly do it"—having formed this resolve, one remains steadfast. (23)
Relying upon that [channel], both the Moon and the Sun set within the path of the Suṣumṇā by way of the upward path,
leaving behind the sphere of the Brahmāṇḍa.
Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved,
the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep.
This is that Devadatta, the knower, who designates the wondrous, existent reality and is unsurpassable.
Having made the resolve: "Whatever my preceptor shall say or command,
that I will certainly do— I shall perform it, I shall carry it out," and having adopted and grasped that state of being which consists of an inclination toward [the goal], he remains focused.

For that man who remains in that state, relying upon it, both the moon and the sun— both the apāna and prāṇa breaths, or the mind and breath— move upward along the path of the equinox (viṣuvat-pravāha) through the suṣumnā path,
the central channel.

Out of curiosity as to what might be in his heart as he himself sets out upon the path of the Supreme Power (*paraśaktimārga*) and goes to dissolution, [the teacher asks]: "Having done what? Having abandoned the sphere of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), having left the domain of the body, and having relinquished the ego-identification with the body (*dehāhaṃbhāva*); [what has he done]?"
The meaning is "having abandoned. And it has been said:
"When the island of the notion of a body has collapsed upon birth, and unity is attained in the stainless ocean of consciousness..."
"Without ever turning back the collection of senses, you, the inner Self of all, shine eternally as the one.
Thus, at that time, in that great void, in the space of supreme consciousness—
When the moon and sun have set, and the functions of knowledge and action have become stilled,
the deluded one— whose own nature remains unmanifest and who is bewildered by dreams and the like— is unawakened and becomes obstructed, as in the state of deep sleep. Just as:
In the state of deep sleep, one who is awakened likewise becomes entirely unobscured. And it is said in the *Rahasyastotra*:
"Within one's own self, the moon and sun are stilled..."

"Even some of those who move through the sky (*khecaras*), whose vision is sharpened by contemplation, remain unable to behold Your abode once they have transcended the path of the heavens. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere, the calming of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths is declared to be the means for the arising of the stainless reality (*nirañjana-tattva*). Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bhogamokṣapradīpikā* that success is attained sequentially within the reality of poison called Kāmākhya, which is also named Nirañjana.
It may be so;
"In the sun and the moon, from the heart, and from their tranquility"—this is the essence of all scripture.
Thus has the arising of the *spandatattva* been proclaimed. And from that very [source], then...
The arising of the mantra is innate (*sahaja*). And it is said in the *Bauddhāyana-saṃhitā*:
"While the moon is in its quiescent state, known as the end of the new moon (*amānta*), and before the sun has risen—this is the arising of all mantras and the dissolution of the gods."
In the *Mālinīvijaya* as well:
"That place where the individual soul (jīva), liberated from its support, shall attain dissolution,
is held to be the field of origin for all mantras."
Likewise,
for one whose mind is restrained within [the interval between] dharma and adharma,
whatever he speaks becomes mantra; how much more so, then, that which arises from the *mātṛkā*?
Thus [ends the section]. 23–24–25.
Therefore,
having taken hold of that power, the mantras— possessing the power of the Omniscient One—
proceed toward their respective functions, just as the sense organs of embodied beings do.

Having ascended— that is, having presided over— that power, which consists of the manifestation of unconditioned consciousness and is called the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), the mantras— consisting of the forms of seeds (*bīja*),
clusters (*piṇḍa*), words (*pada*), and names (*nāma*), and possessing the nature of protecting through contemplation (*manana*)— [attain their efficacy].

Because they are illuminated by the awakening of the power of the innate resonance (*sahajanāda*), these ministers—endowed with the glory of powers such as omniscience—are engaged in their respective offices for the sake of bestowing grace and so forth. How so? Just like the instruments, such as the hands and feet, of an embodied being.
