By this, it is stated that for the practitioner (*mantrin*), through the realization of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), there exists the capacity to employ mantras at will by mere intention alone. As it is said in the *Trikasāra*:
"But when the supreme reality—beyond syllables and indeed formless—is known..."
But the mantras, together with the lords of mantras, become their servants.

Otherwise, however, even those mantras which are applied with effort— because they lack contact with the power of consciousness due to being the locus of previously mentioned conceptualizations and so forth, and because they consist merely of phonemes— are fruitless endeavors, like the act of making a doll.
And it is said in the *Haṃsapārameśvara*:
"Mantras remaining in the state of bound souls (*paśu*) consist solely of the form of phonemes."
When uttered upon the path of the Suṣumṇā, they attain the state of lords.
Since this is the path of power (*śākta*) and herein lies the efficacy of the mantras,
it is stated in the *Tattvarakṣāvidhāna*:
"Because of incapacity and because of being devoid of action, [power] resides neither in the individual soul (*pums*) nor in the supreme state (*pare pade*)."
"One should employ the mantra when [the disciple] is capable; thus, the recitation becomes fruitful.
And in the *Śrīvaihāyasī*: "One should perform the recitation while situated at the equinox (*viṣuvat*), awakened by the resonance of the *nāda* and the upward-sounding vibration."
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being strung upon the power like jewels on a thread.

"And that very [power], nourished by the supreme nectar in the sky of the beyond, reveals the true nature of the Self; thus, the mantra [reveals it] even without an oblation. Thus it is said in the *Śrīkālaparā*.
"Therefore, sound, which consists of resonance and is augmented by conceptual cognition,
being non-different from that which abides in the essential nature of the awakening to mantra, brings about awakening as well.
Furthermore, in the *Saṅkarṣaṇasūtras*:
The nature of consciousness is established solely in its own self, refined by both existence and non-existence;
it is to be known through self-awareness and its sphere of experience transcends primordial nature.
O Brahmin, this source of mantras is known to be of the nature of realization;
those mantras arise, both externally and internally, in the form of phonemes.
The states of the timeless word are like the organs of embodied beings;
when applied at all times, they are perfected through the yoga of vigor.
Thus, because its nature is pure awakening, even a single recitation, whether arising internally or externally, amounts to a hundred thousand repetitions. As it is said in the Jayā:
"Of even a single Lord of Mantras, both when arisen internally and externally..."
"O Sage, know that when there is oneness [of these], that recitation is designated as having the count of one hundred thousand (lakṣa).
By this reasoning, the potency of the mantra has been explained.
He now speaks of their setting, which occurs prior to their rising:
"In that very place, they are completely dissolved, tranquil in form and stainless; together with the mind of the worshipper, they possess the nature of Śiva. (27)

In that very state of their own inherent nature, these mantras completely dissolve and set— along with the practitioner’s mind, which is the cause of their activity, and the will that serves as their substratum— because they follow after it and consist of its power.
And it is said in the *Kālaparā*:

"The powers of the supreme syllable, which proceed from the source (*dhātu*) through various manifestations, have attained the state of phonemes (*varṇa*) within the bodies of letters, emerging from the mouth. Thus.
Of what nature are they? Because they have accomplished all that was to be done, they are peaceful in form;
for this very reason, they are stainless (*nirañjana*), being free from great turbidity, or because they are animated by the stainless reality (*nirañjana-tattva*). And for this same reason—

"Those whose qualities (dharmas)—that is, attributes—are like those of Śiva are 'possessors of Śiva’s nature' (śivadharmiṇaḥ). The meaning is that they are omniscient and omnipotent. In this way, he alone is the essence of the mantra; and for this very reason, their status as possessors of Śiva’s nature is established. || 27 ||
That which is remembered dissolves there together with the mind of the practitioner;
this [state] is Śiva-nature within the self because of the identity with all things, and this is supported by reasoning.

Because the individual soul (jīva) consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being, by virtue of its nature as the consciousness thereof and through the realization of identity with that. || 28 ||
Therefore, among all reflections upon words and their meanings, there is no state that is not Śiva;
for the enjoyer alone is eternally established everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment.
Because the living self (*jīva*) is indeed the Self (*ātman*), consisting of all, having all as its essence, and being universal in form due to its nature as the cognizer.
And it has been said: [The verse follows:]...
At the very moment the universe is known, it is then and there composed of consciousness;
for there is no portion of the object of knowledge, O Lord, that exists outside of the knower.
"The object of cognition attains the state of being a cognizer; the cognizer attains the nature of consciousness.
If consciousness is truly Your self, then this world is composed of You. And so says the Śruti:

"This entire world is indeed the Self; there is nothing whatsoever here that is manifold. Furthermore, the qualification "the source of all beings" contains an implicit reason (*hetugarbha*). Or rather, this is the reason: because [everything] arises from it, [it is the source] of all beings.
Because their origin [is from You]; for their emergence and existence occur through the ascent of consciousness in the form of the supreme word (*parāvāk*) and so forth. As it has been said:
"Your causality is known in everything because of Your pervasive presence."
In a universe endowed with consciousness, non-consciousness cannot be the cause.
"When the sphere of consciousness is known, it attains the designation 'Being' (sat);
by that alone it would not be attained by one who has not cultivated consciousness.
And furthermore:
"No one disputes that all entities have you as their essence;
for that which has entered the state of being manifested does not appear if it is unmanifested. Thus: [The verse continues:

"Just as the sun, though one, appears manifold through its reflection in various vessels filled with water, so too, O Lord, do You, though one, appear as many through Your manifestations in diverse bodies. (ŚvU 6.11)
Creating, speaking, and making known—though one, you are the illuminator in these three ways;
you are distinct from the objects illuminated, unlike other illuminators.
"Without the arising of Your light, luminous things do not shine.
Likewise, in the *Pañcarātra*, it is said: "The sun does not shine there," and so forth.
"...until [the realization that] 'by its light all this is illuminated.
Regarding its being composed of everything (*sarvamayatva*), he states another reason, beginning with "in the perception of that" (*tatsaṃvedane*).

The word "that" (tat) refers to objects of cognition; because their attainment of the nature of being occurs through the medium of experience in the form of their own perception, there arises the realization of identity with them.
From that cause, there arises the consciousness of non-difference from that [object]. For it is said in the *Svātmasaptati*:

"Just as an object, once made an object of knowledge by means of its own nature, attains identity with that [knowledge], so too the individual soul (jīva) becomes identical with all, for it consists of everything."
Elsewhere, in the section on consciousness (*saṃvitprakaraṇa*),
it is said: "Just as everything permeated by fire is seen to be of that [fire's] nature,
so too let everything permeated by knowledge be seen to be of that [knowledge's] nature."
Likewise, in the *Āgamarahasya*, in the section on the letter 'A', it appears above: "This manifestation of that knowledge is also Your own power (*vibhūti*) consisting of the universe."
"That you are the soul of the universe" is not established merely by scripture, but is established even through the nature of one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvidita*).
Thus, consciousness itself assumes the form of speech by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). As it has been said:
When the wind is manifested in the [articulatory] places, speech in its manifest form (vaikharī), which assumes the specific phonemes,
belongs to speakers and is dependent upon the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Merely by taking up the intellect,
the intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk) proceeds, following the form of succession and transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
"But Paśyantī is undivided, with all sequence withdrawn;
she is the light of her own nature within, the subtle, imperishable Speech. Thus [it is said].
And likewise:
He who resounds within himself as the essence of an indistinguishable sound is the Supreme, the Ultimate, the Abiding One, whose innate form is eternally manifest.

"Awakened by the power of consciousness and will, the vibration (spanda), impelled by the strength of the Self, shines within the heart like the sun, gathering all splendors. Thus it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā*. And:
Consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness, is the supreme speech arising from its own inherent savor;
this is the primary sovereignty, the supreme lordship of the Self.
"That vibration is the Great Being, undifferentiated by space or time;
as the very essence, it is declared to be the Heart of the Supreme Lord.
And within that [vibration], which consists of internal discourse, both [subject and object]...
Word and meaning flash forth simultaneously; for this very reason, their non-difference alone is renowned.
And it has been said here:
"For the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of words."
And it has already been stated that speech has consciousness as its root (*saṃvinmūla*)—in the passage beginning with "from the root of consciousness" (*saṃvinmūlāt*).
Furthermore, other things have been stated by verses of a similar kind:
"Just as the entire world has been pierced by you with your own self..."
Thus, when permeated by you, the Goddess of Speech shines forth in every way.
And it has been said by the Lord of Yogins:
"Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing everything, speech is the supreme cause;
it must be sought after because the determination of an object occurs through its superimposition."
The conceptualization of its existence occurs solely through its own orientation toward manifestation;
for without that, O Mother, it could not even attain its own self.
And in that state, she is held to be the light of one's own essential nature (svarūpajyotis),
free from division or succession, accessible to yogis, and conforming to their true form.
Then, through that orientation toward Śiva, speech becomes "consisting of reflection" (cintāmayī),
characterized by the manifestation of the desire to express specific words as its object.
Therefore, by virtue of having sound as its essence, it becomes manifest as consisting of meaning;
for without that very nature [of sound], there can be no determination of meaning.

Thus, the very radiance of consciousness— which is the nature of all-illuminating awareness— is its power of illumination; that which takes the form of internal verbalization (*sañjalpa*), being the life-force of phonemes, words, and sentences, emerges externally as the form of objects.
This is well-established through the direct experience of the awakened ones. And it has been said:
"The Lord, whose very self is consciousness, manifests the multitude of objects existing within Him externally by the power of His will, even without any material substrate, just like a yogi."
The manifestation of the multitude of existents residing within the Self exists indeed for the Lord;
without that, the reflective awareness of will does not proceed.
And it is said elsewhere:
"O Lord, whatever appears externally, all that surely exists within you;
otherwise, how could those with closed eyes perceive everything in their hearts in exactly that same way?"

Thus, since this very nature exists as such through a nature that resides in all selves and belongs to all selves, there is no state whatsoever— whether among the mental deliberations regarding word and meaning, or within the object itself— in which it does not exist.
Śiva manifests his own nature; the meaning is that [the world] is not of the nature of consciousness [independently].

Because of the identity with the appropriation of consciousness (*saṃvit-svīkaraṇa-ekya*), there is the existence of everything. As it has been said: "By whatever cause the rivers of objective entities are divided..."
Having converged in the ocean of awakening, they attain oneness through each and every one of them.
And it was stated previously: "O Lord, there is no worldly convention— whether arising from the body, from speech, or from the mind— in which you are not the foremost."

Therefore, the enjoyer alone—the experiencer alone—is established at all times and in all places as the state of the enjoyed (*bhogya*), by virtue of being that which is experienced; there is no other object of enjoyment. And thus says the Śruti: "I am food, I am food, I am food."
I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food.
The author of the treatise has also stated in the *Tattvavicāra*:
"Entities, established in their own respective natures, are connected with one another through the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer; they are never so by virtue of their intrinsic nature."
"The seer, the experiencer, the rememberer, the grasper, the enjoyer, the feeler, the agent, the perceiver, the knower, and the cognizer—these are the designations for consciousness.
By this, the meaning is that consciousness itself manifests in the form of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). And it has been said:
That which appears as one's own self, though distinct from you— the all-pervading enjoyer— is seen so only through delusion;
such beings are objects of enjoyment for others, like cattle.
They wander further in this existence for the sake of enjoyment.
O Blessed One, by contemplating existence itself as being truly the nature of existence,
they would become partakers of the state of lordship, just like Your Honor.

"They are capable of bringing the entire universe under their control. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Jñānasambodha*: "The knower, the object of knowledge, and knowledge—such is the threefold abiding of knowledge itself."
That which was stated in the verse "The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman," is precisely this.
And it has been stated by me elsewhere: "The seer alone exists; this visible world does not exist. This is known by the wise through inner self-realization (*adhyātma*):
this world, though appearing as if divided into two distinct parts, shines forth like a reflection in a mirror.
These external objects, such as jars and the like, always attain existence through the penetration of consciousness;
therefore, according to the doctrine of the non-duality of knowledge, the existence of the object of cognition does not exist independently anywhere.
Thus, in the *Ātmasaptati*:
"Whatever is seen here does not differ from the act of seeing."
"Vision is not other than the seer; for the world is indeed the seer itself. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Saṅkarṣaṇasūtras*:
"That by which this universe is seen, the one who is always the seer of all..."
"He who is the visible one in the state of the moving and the unmoving is sung as Viṣṇu. Thus it is said.
Also in the Jābāli-sūtras:
"The seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, and the thinker..."
The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, whose nature is consciousness never subject to loss, the sole cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, is the Self;
thus it is stated in the Pañcarātra Upaniṣad.
The knower and the knowable, the speaker and the spoken, the enjoyer and the enjoyable—such is the beginning.
Likewise, in this very [text]: "It is within all and outside all, the self-luminous."
"It is to be awakened by oneself; thus he is the Self-existent (Svayambhū). The Śruti also says:
"He alone is the knower, and that is his knowledge."
In this very context, by way of praise, he states the means of appropriation:
"Or rather, he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play—he, seeing thus, is constantly disciplined and is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (30)
The word "vā" here is used in its own sense. What need is there for much?

Thus, he whose consciousness—his perception or knowledge—is of the aforementioned nature, [perceiving] that "everything is indeed composed of Me," [regards] that entire, complete world as a garden for play.

By perceiving and contemplating [the Self], and through the destruction of ignorance—the cause of bondage—due to being constantly engaged [in practice], one attains awakening; thus, even while living, one is liberated like the Lord. Of this there is no doubt.
Because it is established through both logical proof and direct perception, there is no delusion here.
And it has been said:
"He who remains with unimpaired experience, resting perfectly within his own awakened awareness..."
"Even while enjoying sense objects, he who knows the reality is liberated while living.
As for those who say, "How can there be liberation without the departure [of the soul]?"—to refute that, he says:
"Without the experience of one's own true nature, for the person..."
If liberation were to result from the power of departing [the body],
then even in this view, is it not the case that the deluded person who performs the act of hanging [for suicide] would partake in liberation?
Likewise:
"Even those in Videha are bound at the time of dissolution by the perfuming of the *guṇas*;
yet embodied beings are liberated by taking refuge in pure knowledge. Thus [it is said].

Through the immersion in the cultivation of these two types of concentration— either that "this entire world resides within me, who am the womb of gnosis," or that "I reside everywhere"— [one attains stability].
O Lord of the three worlds, by performing worship unto you, men— whose afflictions and calamities have been shattered— attain [the goal] before long.
Even in the Gītā: "He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—
of him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me."
Also in the *Pañcarātra*:
"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man, beyond grief, looks down upon grieving people;
like one standing on a mountain peak looking at those on the ground, he observes them all."
And here, by means of reasoning, it is implied that the very state of being constantly diligent is the method;
for it was stated previously: "Therefore, one should always be diligent," and so forth. || 30 ||
Now, he provides a conclusion for what was previously stated regarding the nature of the mantra, by way of describing the emergence of another method:
"This very emergence of that object of meditation occurs within the mind of the meditator."
It is the attainment of identity with that [reality] for the practitioner who so desires. (31)

This very [state] is the arising of the meditator’s mind in the form of that aforementioned object of meditation consisting of mantra; it belongs to the practitioner, the meditator, who desires and grasps at *samāpatti*— the state of oneness, the attainment of the nature of mantra.
"Identity with that" means the attainment of the essential nature of the object of meditation; for it is said in the Viśvasaṃhitā:
"When the mind is dissolved into the object of meditation, that is declared to be dhyāna."
The object of meditation becomes manifest, and the meditator attains identity with it.
Alternatively, based on the reading "ṛcchatastu," that attainment of identity with Him which occurs for one who meditates and contemplates here— that oneness is its arising.
The author of the work, however, accepts both as his intended meaning;
for that identification with the deity of the mantra which occurs through the desire to utter the mantra,
and that internal apprehension of its nature by means of inner consciousness consisting of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra— both are intended.
Thus, he states the fruit of this very pervasion, namely the manifestation of this [Self]:
"This alone is the attainment of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self."
And this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true essence of Śiva.
This self-awareness of one's own true nature is the attainment of immortality for the self in this world;
it is not, however, the absence of rebirth due to the cessation of old age and death.
"This very [initiation] is the spontaneous grace bestowed upon oneself by Him who has emerged from the Ocean of Milk;
it is the initiation of liberation, and it is that which unites one with the Supreme Self. Thus [it is said].
And it is said in the *Mokṣadharmas*:

"Having abandoned all conceptual constructions, one should fix the mind upon the sentient being (*sattva*). When the mind is dissolved into the sentient being, then one becomes a conqueror of time. Thus it is said.
And for the sake of one's own awakening, there shall surely be the cessation of existences; indeed, the knowledge of intrinsic nature is already known to men.
"By merely consuming nectar once, it brings immortality to mortal beings.
This is for the purpose of initiation.
It bestows the true essence of knowledge and exhausts all impurity;
initiation is said to have the nature of giving and destroying because it pierces through with awakening.
Thus [ends the section]. 32.
Having proclaimed the arising of the reality of Spanda as being uncreated right there,
he then spoke of the arising of mantra, its potency, and its manifestations.
In order to state that the sovereignty [of the subject] exists in dream as well— just as it exists in the waking state through the attainment of its own nature as previously described— he says:
"Just as the Creator, when requested by desire, [manifests] objects situated in the heart for one who is awake..."
Having brought about the rising of the moon and the sun, he brings [liberation] to embodied beings.
Likewise, because it never fails to fulfill desired objects even in dreams,
that which stands in the middle must necessarily manifest itself most clearly and constantly.
Just as in the waking state, the Creator—

the Ordainer whose very nature is the Self— being entreated and requested by the embodied person with a desire consisting of the wish to see, [reveals] the unmanifested objects situated within the heart of that person.
It brings about and illuminates the categories of existence by relying on its own power.

Having done what? Having brought about the rising of the moon and the sun—that is, of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths, as well as the two eyes—meaning by means of the application [of awareness] to the eyes and other senses.

This is what is meant: even when many objects are present—such as among courtesans, actors, wrestlers, or spectators—one perceives only that specific object which is intended, because [the mind] enters into its own nature. Likewise...
Remaining in his own essential nature within the heart, he constantly and eternally makes manifest—that is, reveals—only those objects desired even in dreams, making them exceedingly clear.
Why? Because there is no transgression of, that is, no abandonment of, *praṇaya*, which here means the fulfillment of one's wishes or requests.

"When, having abandoned the firm desire for what is desired, there is no other mental state"—this means that if desire follows only its object and does not arise independently, then this [state] occurs; and he (the subject) does not transcend that [desire]. And it has been said:
O Knower of All, just as one who applies himself to a forgotten meaning quickly recovers it through diligent study,
so too, whatever is requested by this [devotee] with such passion, you will not fail to fulfill it, even if it were to occur only in a dream.
Thus it is said; and it is stated by the Siddhas:
"That which one situated in the space of consciousness contemplates, that one perceives as undivided."
In the science of astrology as well: "By whichever sense-object a person is pierced when he sleeps,
it is that very sense-object whose activities he perceives while asleep."
Thus [ends the section]. 33–34.

Thus, by means of describing the sovereignty of dream, the piercing of the veil of deep-sleep darkness has been explained through reasoning. Now, he says [the following] in order to declare that sovereignty exists only for one who abides in his own true nature during waking, dreaming, and so forth, and not otherwise:
Otherwise, however, creation would be independent because it possesses that nature [of independence], just as in the case of an ordinary person in both the states of waking and dreaming. (35)

Otherwise, however, in the absence of the mind’s abiding in its own true nature, because of its flickering nature, the creation occurring in dreams and so forth would be independent in the form of mere will.
The meaning is that the expansion of dreams and such would become inconsistent with reality.

Why is that? Because it possesses that nature, because its inherent nature is emission (*sṛṣṭi*). For that reality is eternally characterized by the creative flow known as will (*icchā*). Of what is it like?
It is like [the experience] of an ordinary person of unawakened mind, who constantly [perceives] within the two states of waking and dreaming.

At all times, the will to create is indeed independent; for it does not arise from a state of non-awakening. It is connected to him in thousands of ways, appearing solely as the form of conceptual constructions that are both bound and unbound.
That is to say, it would exist even in both states. || 35 ||

Having thus explained the reasoning known as "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*) regarding the manifestations of the Self, he now describes therein that which is known as the capacity for the activity of knowledge— the means for knowing subtle, concealed, and other such objects.
He states this with two verses:
"For just as an object seen indistinctly, even when the mind is attentive, appears much more clearly later on when cultivated through the exertion of its own power. (36)
For instance, when some object— a specific thing such as a jar or a cloth— is seen indistinctly and with doubt while standing at a distance,
even though the mind is attentive, free from other distractions, and one-pointed.

That very same object, when further cultivated and investigated through the exertion of one's own power— that is, through a specific effort of the self— shines forth most clearly; it manifests and appears free from all doubt.

Therefore, whatever object exists in a certain manner, with a certain form, at a certain place, and at a certain time— that very object, in that same way and by that very means, through a specific effort, [discloses] its own power, its own essential nature.

Having pervaded, taken hold of, and firmly grasped that which is blossoming, through practice it soon—that is, quickly—manifests itself perfectly; it shines forth clearly because its own nature is free from obscuration.

For it has been stated previously: [The Sanskrit verse follows: ... [as cited in the source] ... (Note: The specific Sanskrit verse was not provided in the input text, so the translation reflects the commentary's explanation.)
Moreover, through the touch of his own power, a person may become equal to him;
and regarding the application of reality,
O Pārvatī, he who knows by means of which [means] one becomes a sovereign over the sense objects.
He who knows that in its true essence has known the entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
Having thus described such knowledge— which, because it pertains to the past and the future, has a limited scope— as being nothing at all wonderful,
[the author] now speaks for the sake of overcoming the power of agency and its capacity to act.
He states another expedient:
"Since even one who is weak proceeds toward his task by overcoming that [weakness], so too should one who is excessively hungry conceal his hunger. (38)

Even one who is weak, whose constituent elements are depleted, incapable, and emaciated, proceeds toward his task and accomplishes his activity by seizing— that is, by taking hold of and assuming— that strength characterized by enthusiasm and consisting of exertion.
Because even one who is extremely emaciated may display power in battle and similar situations by relying on the strength of exertion;
this is what is meant: just as someone, though initially incapable, attains great power through the force of effort by means of the practice of physical exercise.

Likewise, even one who is extremely hungry and afflicted by hunger may, through that very cultivation of his own true nature, cover over the desire to eat— that is, the longing for food— and thus pacify the hunger. And it has been said:
By means of Patañjali,
there is the cessation of hunger and thirst at the throat-pit; likewise,
by means of the powers (*balas*), there are the powers of an elephant and so forth.
The word "hunger" (bubhukṣā) here is used as an illustration; by this, it is meant that the six waves—namely hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death—are also destroyed.
Thus, not only does he possess omniscience and other qualities in this very body, but they exist everywhere as well; so, by way of an expedient means, he says:
"Just as omniscience and other qualities exist in a body presided over by him..."
Likewise, by presiding over one's own self, it will be so everywhere. || 39 ||
When this body is presided over— that is, pervaded and observed— by this aforementioned nature of the Self, qualities such as omniscience and so forth are found to exist;
for by means of this, one perceives even the eating of a tiny louse or similar creature here with immediate clarity.
And it is said in the *Jñānasambodha*:
"Because of its pervasiveness, he alone is all; by his very nature, he is the Knower;
and because he is omniscient, the Person alone is designated as the Omniscient One."
Furthermore: If you were not omniscient at all times within the heart of everyone,
by what means could it be possible for him to have memories whose objects are things that have perished?
Where did infants born on that very day learn to suckle at the breast, or how did living beings learn to cross the waters? This is the deed of the Omniscient One.
Furthermore:
"What might be edible and what inedible? What sweet and what not sweet?"—in such a determination, how could flies possess consciousness regarding the act of collecting honey?
Otherwise, even for an all-knowing controller,
the production of those with bodies as small as mere worms would be a cause for wonder.
An elephant casts away the fruit of the *kataka* tree with the desire to clarify the water; for what is this wisdom of an ignorant beast?
Can the discernment to listen to songs be attributed to a deer of simple intellect,
by virtue of which its state of standing still would cease its rumination?
"How will he devour me while I am thus situated in the hole of a mouse? What suspicion can there be regarding the cat, other than the proclamation of the Omniscient One?"
Out of fear, that tortoise withdraws all its limbs within its shell;
what is there to wonder at in the undiscriminating intellect of one whose mind is difficult to penetrate?
Beholding the distinct superiority of those whose wings are not yet worn away, he remains devoid of consciousness.
The peacock begins its dance; that is the throbbing of the Teacher of the World.
By whom was the characteristic of devouring fish situated in the midst of unfathomable waters observed, without inference from that [very] water?
Whose is this impossible power? It belongs to the swan drinking water from the lake, and not to that [power] residing within the heart.
Why would even the Knower of the Field (the soul) not understand the cries of the cock dwelling within the temple at the break of dawn?

From that [source], the reckoning of time proceeds at the beginning of the day for one who knows the divisions of time and has performed the ritual procedures without error, intent upon the calculation of those [units].
Since the horns, teeth, claws, and so forth of living beings serve as their weapons,
by whom were these taught to those lacking consciousness, for the sake of excessive striking against others?
A lion knows its own powerful strength and majesty;
what is the cause [of its hesitation] as long as its internal conviction does not manifest with vigor?
It is not surprising that even beasts and birds indicate through their gestures the signs of excessive rain or drought.

"How can there be joy for living beings from lions and other such creatures who are like Death itself, except through the firm establishment of a mutual exchange of consciousness with the One residing in the heart?
And their particular manifestation occurs according to the reasoning previously stated; likewise:

The meaning is that, through presiding over one's own self—that is, by not falling away from one's own essential nature—all qualities such as omniscience will come to be and attain manifestation everywhere. And it has been said:
"A single entity is the essential nature of all entities."
For all phenomena have the nature of a single phenomenon;
by whomsoever one phenomenon is seen in its true reality, by him all phenomena are seen in their true reality.
The secret principle here is this: wherever in the body one may attain firmness of consciousness, there the emergence of qualities occurs. Thus it is said.
Now, for the purpose of severing the root that conceals these qualities, he says:

"Lassitude (*glāni*), which consists of the destruction of joy and lack of enthusiasm, is indeed a ravager and destroyer within the body; and the course, the path, or the arising of that lassitude comes from ignorance."

And when that ignorance is dissolved, cleansed away, and destroyed by the nature of the Self— whose characteristics will be described hereafter— then from where could that exhaustion arise? What indeed would be its cause?
The meaning is that [the body] would become free [from these]. For this very reason, for yogins there is an absence of old age, disease, and so forth, as well as firmness of the body. || 40 ||

He states the essential nature of *unmeṣa*: "That from which the arising of another [thought] occurs for one who is intent upon a single thought—that indeed should be known as *unmeṣa*; one should perceive it for oneself. (41)
For one who is intent upon a single reflection, with the mind engaged in a single object, because of which [object],
there would arise— the manifestation— from its own nature, of another reflection; suddenly.

Since another thought— such as the recollection of what was forgotten— arises [from it], that opening (*unmeṣa*) should be known as the cause of that thought. Furthermore, one should observe and recognize that very opening by oneself within the interval between two thoughts.
The meaning is that, because it is experienced as all-pervasive and is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*), it is inexpressible, like the bliss of a young virgin (*bṛhatkumārīsukha*). || 41 ||
And regarding this [practice], when it is being cultivated, he states the conditions:
"From this, the *bindu*; from this, the *nāda*; from this, the *rūpa*; and from this, the *rasa*—these manifest very quickly for the embodied being as causes of agitation. (42)
Therefore, from this unfolding being cultivated, in a very short time, the *bindu* and other [principles] arise and manifest within the embodied soul;
the *bindu*, whose nature is light, [manifests] in the space between the eyebrows and so forth.

The unartificial *nāda*, consisting of the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound, known as the Brahman of Sound (*śabdabrahman*), and hearing from afar; form, which is seeing in the darkness, the vision of deities, and the perception of subtle objects and so forth; taste—
There is the taste of nectar in the mouth and the six flavors; how do these function as agitators and as obstacles to the attainment of supreme perfection? And so says Patañjali:
From that, prescience, clairaudience, the sense of touch, clairvoyance, the sense of taste, and the power of hearing voices arise.
These are obstacles in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), but they are perfections (*siddhis*) in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
Furthermore, by this reasoning, the sequence of creation and so forth is implied; for:

Emanation has been described as occurring prior to its initial manifestation. How does that [manifestation] occur? Therefore, in those such as ourselves, it takes the form of the expansion of the powers of *bindu*, will (*icchā*), and vision (*dṛk*). From that arises *nāda*, which consists of sound, is called speech (*vāk*), and is of the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). From that arises form.
The nature of the investigation into the perception of objects consists of this very thing. Therefore, in that very context, "rasa" (flavor) is desire in the form of enjoyment;
this indeed is the manifestation of the exertion of those who know the meaning of the most secret sequence.
The sequence of the fourfold process, consisting of chewing and dissolving, has been stated right here by means of reasoning alone;
for a specific rule does not override the general context.
Thus, it was said: "One should personally observe that. (42)
To the question "How is that so?", he states the means here:
(43) When one abides pervading all objects as if with a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand it by oneself.

The desire to see is *didṛkṣā*; when one remains, having pervaded and presided over all objects and all states of being as if situated in that very condition, then what is the use of much speaking or further explanation? [One acts] by oneself, by means of the Self alone.
The meaning is that he will perceive, understand, and know each respective nature.

This is the intended purport of the instruction here: just as one who desires to see out of curiosity remains in a state of blossoming activity, so too does one who abides in the essential nature of the subjectivity (*udyantṛtā*) which consists in the orientation toward all things.

He himself attains that intrinsic nature, which is the locus of qualities such as omniscience; for it was stated previously [in the verse] beginning with "therefore, he is constantly diligent. And this very state is called the "secret mudrā" in the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*. Thus I have said.
In the *Bhogamokṣapradīpikā*:
By the power of the rising [consciousness], through the function of expansion, the yogi should remain established in his own true nature;
having drawn near the objects of the senses by himself, he does not consume them, abiding on the plane of bliss.
This [mudrā], which is unrestrained in form and most fully blossomed for those of awakened intellect, is established as always present therein; indeed, it is the supreme mudrā, delighting in bliss.
And it is said elsewhere:
Having simultaneously cast all powers— beginning with vision— toward their respective objects of knowledge in every direction by means of the mind,
[he remains] in the center like a pillar of gold.
Standing as the sole support of all, you shine forth.
Likewise,
those whose eyes and other senses are as fickle as a courtesan wandering at will here and there like a common woman— [those are the ones who fall].
Seeing only the powers, one should not follow after them; you shine while sustaining the universe within them.
Thus [ends verse] 43.
Regarding this very state, he states the reasoning:
"The awakened one should always remain, having scrutinized the field of experience with knowledge;
he should unify everything in one place, and thereby he is not afflicted by anything else. (44)

Awakened, with his power uncontracted and free from conceptual construction, he should remain and abide at all times as the nature of the impeller; having perceived and delimited the object within the sphere of knowledge,
he should dissolve the knowable into non-differentiation through the radiance of consciousness.
The meaning is "having led [him]. And it was said by me myself in the *Bhogamokṣapradīpikā*:

"Alternatively, having dissolved the nectar of the object of knowledge through the blazing fire of the awakening to non-duality, he who drinks it, becomes satiated, wanders about free from disease, and soon remains forever alone."
This essence of the meaning of the sequence, which is the stage of the supreme flow of the powers,
has been told here by me through his permission for the awakening of good disciples.
Therefore, that consciousness is partless. For it has been said:
"Place, time, action, and form are the well-known causes of division;
therefore, for that which possesses division, by what could it be produced?"
Furthermore: The mind, together with its objects, is the fuel to be burned; the fire of knowledge should burn it away through insights.
Thus, concentration (samādhi), being directed both inwardly and outwardly, is accomplished.
In the same way,
the blazing submarine fire of consciousness, by its own power, incessantly devours the ocean of knowable objects;
no other [element] would possess the capacity to swallow it.

"Neither by the non-attainment nor by the attainment of abundant waters is one's thirst quenched; that which possesses the state of having accomplished its purpose is something unique—the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha).
This has already been explained at length with supporting arguments. For the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything.

And so forth. In this way, one should superimpose everything upon the single reality-svabhāva—which is of the nature of *vidyā* and consists of gnosis—and lead it to unity. Therefore, [it] is not [to be understood] by means of any other collection of *kalās* to be described hereafter, which are of the nature of *śakti* and consist of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
It is not afflicted, nor is it obstructed; the meaning is that it is not displaced from its own nature. And it has been said:
"The one, all-pervading space, due to its connection with walls and other such things..."
Thus, your concentration— unimpaired by the distraction of the grasper and the grasped— perceives you as a single reality, appearing both as the internal subject and the external object.
Thus [ends the section]. 44.
Thus, the awakened Lord is not afflicted by anything else;
however, he who is unawakened is a bound soul (paśu) and is destroyed.
It is now stated what that [bound soul] is and what its characteristics are:
Having become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds,
and having had his sovereign power eclipsed by *kalā*, he is known as a bound soul (*paśu*).

The "mass of words" (śabdarāśi) is a collection of sounds; it is the *mātṛkā*, the mother of words, consisting of the assembly of phonemes from *a* to *kṣ*. Since words consist of phonemes, [this applies] to that which arises from them, namely the groups of consonants beginning with *ka*.

When the power and majesty of the wheel of energies beginning with Brāhmī have been eclipsed by the letters beginning with *ka* through their respective *kalās*, and his great pervasiveness has been stolen away, he is displaced from his true nature; consequently, having become an object of enjoyment, the *puruṣa* is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*).
Because of ignorance. And it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"The subject is called the Lord (*pati*) with respect to entities that are the form of his own limbs;
through *māyā*, he is the bound soul (*paśu*), defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth, with respect to those [entities] that appear as separate."
And in some cases, upon the dissolution of the knot of duality, one attains the identity of karma and the Self.
When this is not realized, he is called a bound soul (paśu); when it is realized, he is indeed the Lord (pati).
Thus [ends the section]. 45.
And therefore:
"The loss of the supreme nectar-essence for him arises from that which is born of causal conditions;
by means of that, he falls into a state of dependence, and that [loss] has as its object only those [conditions]. (46)

And that arising of cognition in the sacrificial animal— namely, the production of knowledge such as memory through the perception of objects by means of the doors of the ears and other senses— is itself the "fall" (*apāya*), which is the deviation from the emergence of one's own true nature due to the supreme nectar. For by that [fall], he...
The person (pumān) attains—reaches—a state of lack of independence and dependence, as well as non-omnipresence and so forth.

And that [state] arises from cognition; its scope consists of those [subtle elements] alone, meaning it has objects such as sound and the rest as its domain and is characterized by desire for them. || 46 ||
And for this very reason:
"Even when its own nature is obscured, its powers are perpetually active, because the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of words. (47)
And regarding this person, the powers previously mentioned— Brahmī and the others— which consist of sound and serve to veil his true nature by concealing his own essential being,
are constantly active and ever-present through the medium of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
For the purpose of obscuring the male form: because there is no arising of cognition— that is, no experience of knowledge— without the interpenetration of sound and the succession of phonemes,
since the object of a word is dependent upon sound.
And because the signified and the signifier mutually illuminate one another, it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"There is no cognition in the world that does not follow from the accompaniment of words."
"All knowledge appears as if permeated by sound. Thus [it is said].
For it was stated previously: "Speech alone is the cause of its universal activity," and so forth;
and furthermore:
"If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, then manifestation itself would not manifest, for it is that [nature] which performs reflective awareness. (47)
Now he explains that this very power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is the cause of both bondage and liberation:

"This same power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva while residing in the bound soul (*paśu*), is the binder; when it abides in its own path and is known [as such], it bestows success, the initiatory rites, and so forth. (48)

This very power (śakti), which consists of action (kriyā) and has action as its nature, which binds the ignorant and generates bondage— O Blessed One, that same [power] exists in Śiva, who is perfectly awakened, abiding within the bound soul (paśu) in such a way that he may be employed at will, just like a bound soul.

She exists as described. And she, when known to be one's own and established in her own path, brings about accomplishment; that is to say, she bestows both supreme and non-supreme accomplishments and leads to enjoyment and liberation. By implication, however, if she is known to be different [from oneself], she becomes a giver of bondage.
Alternatively, this is another explanation: "She is this," and so forth, which has the same meaning as the previous one.

Abiding on her own path, she is independent; when unknown, she is a binder, but when known, she brings about accomplishment (*siddhi*). And this was stated previously: [that] by which the falling of living beings occurs.
By [the passage] beginning with "thus," etc. || 48 ||

To clarify how this [consciousness] becomes the cause of bondage, he says: "Obstructed by the *puryaṣṭaka*—which consists of the emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and resides within the mind, ego, and intellect—it experiences the arising of cognitions produced from that. (49)
It is said that the *puryaṣṭaka* has two forms:
one is subtle, known as the *ātivāhika*, consisting of the *tanmātras* and characterized by expression;
the second is gross, composed of the elements, and known as the *bhoga*. Among these, by means of the subtle...

Constrained, bound, and enveloped by the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), and therefore being under the control of another, it experiences—that is, consumes—the enjoyment consisting of the perception of pleasure and pain arising from the cognitions produced by that [puryaṣṭaka]. Of what nature is this? It is [the experience] of the subtle elements (tanmātra).

That which arises through the medium of the experience of sound and the other [objects]—that is its manifestation (rūpa); by that [manifestation], and likewise by that which resides in the mind, ego, and intellect, conjoined with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). And of that [puryaṣṭaka]:

Due to its existence and under its influence, the embodied soul wanders; it goes through the cycle of transmigration. Therefore, we declare and explain this very thing to be the cause and the reason for this dissolution of transmigration—the stream of birth and death. (49–50)
Having thus described the cause of bondage, he states the means for its cessation:
"But when [the mind] is firmly established in one place, then by restraining its dissolution and emergence, it attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, it becomes the Lord of the Wheel. (51)
Thus,
through the investigation into bondage and liberation, [it is said] "when again" (yadā punaḥ),
referring to when [the soul] resides within one or another of the two *puryaṣṭakas*— specifically, within the gross *puryaṣṭaka*.
Or, when he has become firmly established as the subject within the subtle [element], his mind being absorbed therein, he then— by his own will—

governs and brings about at his pleasure the emergence and dissolution, that is, the appearance and disappearance, of the sound and its object which arise from that [subtle element] and are produced by the corresponding cognition.

He attains the state of an enjoyer; he obtains sovereignty; the meaning is that he is liberated from the state of being a bound soul (paśu), which consists of the nature of the object of enjoyment. As it has been said:
"Having become the lord of bound souls, he shall indeed become the lord of bound souls."
"One is immediately liberated from the state of being a bound soul (paśu) upon becoming the Lord of Paśupati. And in the *Svabodhodayamañjarī*:
"Whatever is captivating, once it has come within the range of the eyes..."
"One should cultivate one-pointedness until it is absorbed and brings about cessation.

This being so, the meaning is that through the attainment of sovereignty, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara), the master of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), endowed with omniscience and other qualities, and the sovereign lord of all. || 51 ||

Thus, what was stated regarding his sovereignty over the wheels of power (*śakticakra*) in the first verse is also [present] here. Now, following the completion of the work in this manner, the author praises the words of his Guru out of the force of great joy, while instructing his disciples in the right conduct (*nīti*).
I pay homage to that wondrous speech of the Guru, whose words and meanings are diverse, which serves as a boat for crossing the unfathomable ocean of doubt. 52.
I pay homage to that speech of the Guru. Of what sort is it?

It is that which carries one across the ocean of difficult-to-traverse doubts. Furthermore, it is that which possesses wonderful meanings—namely, the subjects to be expressed—and wonderful words—namely, the sounds themselves.
As has been stated, for this very reason I praise the wondrous and marvelous Sarasvatī of the Teacher; for there is none other more venerable than the Guru. As it is said in the *Jayā*:
"Since the Lord of the World, having assumed a mortal body..."
"By means of the hand of the scripture, he uplifts the great worlds out of compassion.
And in the *Nāradasaṃgraha*:
"One should give the teacher a fee consisting of one's entire property, or even half of it."
"Or else, one's entire wealth—or even a very small amount—should be given for the sake of uprooting saṃsāra. Thus it was said by me [in some place]:
"He who desires to attain the Blessed One must seek out a guru from whom [that attainment may come]."
The Blessed One is known through the scripture, and the scripture is known through the teacher.
"Through the awakening to that [truth], by the dissolution of [false] knowledge, and upon the attainment of true knowledge, he is indeed attained.
Therefore, the Guru is said to be weightier than the scriptures and even the Lord. Thus it is stated in the *Pañcarātra* as well.
Just as the function resides in the Blessed One alone as the speaker. || 52 ||
Now, by means of describing the sequence of oral tradition, the author of the compendium attaches his own name in a verse for the sake of proclaiming his own fame:
"Having obtained this from the Guru Vasugupta, who perceives the true nature of reality..."
The illustrious Bhaṭṭakallaṭa has correctly versified this secret. || 53 ||

The meaning of this has already been stated at the very beginning, so it is not repeated here. Furthermore, one should not sow this seed of the knowledge of Brahman in an unsuitable place without first examining it; for it has been said by this very author elsewhere:

"Even if it is endowed with qualities, a perfected vidyā given like a maiden to one devoid of qualities brings dishonor upon the giver because it lacks enjoyment; therefore, one should give it to one who possesses those same qualities. (53)
Thus, for the sake of those standing in the darkness of ignorance, this has been illuminated—
shining with pure and stainless qualities like the perfect instruction of the virtuous.
[However, this *Spandapradīpikā* was composed not for the sake of deceiving others by pretending to be a scholar, but rather through the power of the blossoming of pure speech.]
Therefore, having cast aside stinginess and having reflected upon wealth as wealth,
the noble ones should not show disregard for this [gift], which is truly marvelous.

[The son of the one named Trivikrama, born of the station of Nārāyaṇa and known as Utpala, was of noble birth; may this commentary composed by me for the benefit of his excellent disciples serve to dispel the darkness.]
Just as the movement of one holding a lamp at night does not falter anywhere, so he who has wisdom in his hand does not stumble anywhere,
even upon a wrong path.
This *Pradīpikā* is a skillful illuminator.

What is the use of many words? Having plunged into this Sarasvatī of mine— which flows from the supreme tree of awakening, is joined with the further shore, and is perfectly clear— a mortal attains the state of a wise deity.
Even this—remaining here without having abandoned the body—is a marvel; what could be more wonderful than this?
[Thus ends the Spandapradīpikā composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva.]
May there be auspiciousness.
